div.p: Introduction

Of those things, Syrus, which prepare a man to foretell the future through astronomy, two are the greatest and most authoritative. The first, in both order and power, is that by which we apprehend the configurations of the movements of the sun, moon, and stars as they occur from time to time in relation to one another and to the earth. The second is that by which, through the natural character proper to these configurations, we examine the changes they bring about in the things they enclose. The first of these has a study desirable in and for its own sake, even if the end attained by joining it to the second is not reached; and it has been set out for you, as far as was possible, demonstratively, in a treatise of its own. The second, which is not in the same way self-complete, we shall now treat in a manner befitting philosophy, and as one who keeps the love of truth most of all in view: he will not set its apprehension beside the certainty of the first, which is firm and always uniform, since he reckons with the weakness and difficulty of conjecture inherent in much of material quality; nor again will he shrink from inquiry into what is possible, since most of the more general events declare so plainly their cause from the surrounding heavens. But since everything that is hard to attain readily acquires, among the many, a nature easy to disparage, and since, of the two apprehensions set before us, the attacks upon the former would be wholly blind, while those upon the second find ready pretexts for their occasions—for either the difficulty of observation in some matters has produced the opinion of complete impossibility, or the difficulty of guarding what is known, together with the discrediting of the end as useless, has dragged it down—we shall try, before the detailed instruction, to examine in brief the measure both of what is possible and of what is useful in such prediction; and first of what is possible.
Introduction

The more authoritative of the matters set out beforehand in tabular form have now been treated by us, as in summary, up to this point, with a view to the examination of particular predictions. Let us now join to them, in the order that follows, the several inquiries that fall within the scope of what is possible in such prediction, holding throughout to instruction by way of the natural method.

Prognostication through astronomy is divided into two greatest and most authoritative parts. The first and more general is that taken with respect to whole nations, countries, and cities, which is called the universal; the second and more particular is that with respect to each single man, which is itself called the genethlialogical. We think it fitting to speak first of the universal, since these things are by nature changed by greater and stronger causes than the things accomplished in particulars. And since the weaker natures are always subject to the more powerful, and particulars to universals, it would be wholly necessary for those who choose to examine any single thing to have grasped, much earlier, the matters of broader scope.

Of the universal examination itself, one part again is taken with respect to whole countries, another with respect to cities. And further, one part deals with the greater and more periodic circumstances, such as wars, famines, plagues, earthquakes, floods, and the like; another with the lesser and more seasonal, such as the changes of the yearly seasons in their greater or lesser degree, the slackenings or intensifications of winters, heats, and winds, fruitfulness and barrenness, and such things. Reasonably, both of these have as their forerunner that which concerns whole countries and the greater circumstances, for the same reason as that already stated.

For the examination of these, two things especially are taken up: the kinship of the twelve signs of the zodiac, and further that of the stars, with the several climes; and the significations that occur from time to time in the regions proper to them—according to the eclipses, in the conjunctions of sun and moon, and according to the passages of the wandering stars, in their risings and stations. We shall set out beforehand the natural account of the sympathies mentioned, presenting at the same time, in a cursory way, the bodily and ethical characteristics observed, generally speaking, among whole nations, which are not foreign to the natural constitution of the stars and signs kindred to them.
Introduction

The examination concerning universal events having been treated by us in what precedes, as being prior and able in most cases to overrule what is accomplished, in keeping with the particular nature, for each single man—the predictive part of which we call genethlialogical—it is fitting to hold that the power of both kinds is one and the same, both in respect of what is productive and in respect of what is theoretical. For the cause both of universal and of individual events is the movement of the wandering stars, the sun, and the moon; while the predictive part is the scientific observation, through the surrounding heavens, of the turning of the underlying natures in accordance with the similar-figured passages of the heavenly bodies—except that the universal circumstance is greater and self-complete, while the particular is not so in the same way. The beginnings, however, are no longer to be reckoned the same for both, from which, supposing the disposition of the heavenly bodies, we try to foreknow the things signified through the configurations then existing. Rather, of the universal events there are many beginnings, since we do not have one for the whole; and these too are not always taken from the underlying subjects themselves, but also from the surrounding heavens that bring on the causes, for we examine nearly all of them from the more complete eclipses and the conspicuous passages of the stars. But of the events for each single man there is both one and many: one, the beginning of his very compounding—for this too we have; and many, the significations of the surrounding heavens that befall in succession with respect to the first beginning—the one here, however, being reasonably prior, since it itself accomplishes the others. This being so, from the first beginning are observed the universal characteristics of the compounding, and through the others the things that will befall from time to time in greater or lesser degree, according to the so-called divisions of the times that follow.

The temporal beginning of human births being, by nature, that of the very sowing of the seed, but, in power and by what accompanies, that of the bringing-forth at birth: for those who know the time of the sowing, whether by chance or also by observation, it is more fitting to follow that beginning with a view to the characteristics both of the body and of the soul, examining the productive power of the configuration of the stars at it. For once at the beginning the seed has become of a certain quality from the influence of the surrounding heavens, even though this become different through the successive times of the body's formation, it, naturally adding to itself its own proper material alone, in the course of growth is still more assimilated to the characteristic of the first quality. But for those who do not know it—which is what generally happens—it is necessary to attend to the beginning at the bringing-forth, and to give heed to this, as being itself also greatest and falling short of the first in this alone, that through the first the things even before the bringing-forth can be foreknown. For if one would call the one the beginning, and the other, as it were, the inception, its magnitude becomes in time second, but in power equal and even more complete; and one might almost justly name the former the genesis of human seed, the latter that of the man. For the infant then takes on many things that were not present to it before, when it was in the womb, and these the very things proper to human nature alone, and the bodily configuration; and even though the surrounding circumstance at the bringing-forth seem to contribute nothing toward its being of such a kind, yet this very thing—that it came to light at the configuration proper to the surrounding heavens—contributes, since nature, after the completion, makes the impulse of its exit toward a condition of like form to that which formed it in particular at the beginning. So that one may reasonably hold that the configuration of the stars at the bringing-forth is significant of such things, not, however, as wholly productive, but as having, of necessity and by nature, that which is most like, in power, to the productive.

Since our present purpose is to fill up this part too by way of method, according to the reckoning set forth at the beginning of this treatise concerning the possibility of such prognostication, we shall pass over the ancient manner of predictions, which is according to the conjoint blending of all or most of the stars, as being manifold and almost boundless if one should wish to treat it accurately in detail, and as able to be examined rather in the particular applications of those who inquire naturally than in mere traditions, both because it is hard to use and hard to set out in full. The practices themselves, through which each of the kinds is discerned according to the method of application, and the productive powers of the stars toward each thing—taken in their characteristic and more comprehensive form—we shall set out as consequentially as may be and at the same time concisely, according to natural conjecture: laying down beforehand the places of the surrounding heavens to which each of the human events is referred, like a mark at which one must aim; fitting the productive powers, in their more comprehensive form, of the bodies kindred to the places by prevalence, as it were like the shootings of arrows; and leaving the event, gathered together from the blending of several natures concerning the underlying kind, to the reckoning of him who examines, as to a skilled archer. And first we shall make our account concerning the universal characteristics observed through the beginning at the bringing-forth, in the order that is fitting; all things, as we said, that have a nature able to be taken through this beginning—those who wish to busy themselves further with the characteristics belonging to the compounding alone, and with the characteristics that fall under examination at the time of the sowing, contributing through the same theory.
Preface

The matters that can be examined before birth, those that belong to the birth itself, and further those things after birth that pertain to the constitution and reveal the general quality of the temperament — these are roughly all that we have treated. Of the things that befall a person from outside, and that ought to be examined in their order, the account of acquisitive and dignitary fortune comes first; and just as acquisitive fortune is bound up with the conditions of the body, so dignitary fortune is bound up with those of the soul.
That knowledge through astronomy is attainable, and how far

That a certain power is diffused and reaches from the ethereal and eternal nature over all the region about the earth, which is wholly subject to change—the first elements beneath the moon, fire and air, being themselves enclosed and altered by the motions in the ether, while they in turn enclose and jointly alter all the rest, earth and water and the plants and animals in them—this would appear most clearly and in a few words to everyone. For the sun, together with the surrounding heavens, always disposes in some way all the things about the earth, not only through the changes that accompany the yearly seasons—bringing about the generation of animals, the fruitfulness of plants, the flowing of waters, and the alterations of bodies—but also through its daily circuits, warming, moistening, drying, and cooling in an ordered manner and in accordance with its positions relative to the point overhead us. The moon, too, as the body nearest the earth, distributes most of her effluence upon the earth, since most things, whether without soul or with soul, are in sympathy with her and change along with her: the rivers swell and ebb their streams with her lights, the seas turn their own movements with her risings and settings, and plants and animals are filled out and diminished with her, either wholly or in some of their parts. The passages of the stars, both the fixed and the wandering, likewise produce many signs in the surrounding heavens—of heat, of wind, of snow—by which the things upon the earth too are accordingly disposed. And further, the configurations they form to one another, as their distributions come together and are blended, work out very many and varied changes: the power of the sun prevailing as regards the ordering of quality as a whole, while the rest cooperate with it or work against it in some respect; the moon doing so more evidently and more continuously, as in her conjunctions, half-moons, and full moons; the stars more periodically and less perceptibly, as in their appearances, occultations, and approaches. If these things are viewed in this way, it would seem to everyone to follow that not only are things already compounded necessarily disposed in some way by the motion of these bodies, but also that the beginnings and formations of the seeds are molded and shaped to the quality proper to the surrounding heavens at that time. The more observant of farmers and herdsmen, at any rate, conjecture from the winds that occur at the times of mating and of sowing the seed the quality of what will come to pass. And in general we see that the more comprehensive matters—signified by the more conspicuous configurations of sun, moon, and stars—are foreknown for the most part even by those who reason not scientifically but only by observation: those that come from a greater power and a simpler order being known even by the wholly untaught, and indeed even by some of the irrational animals, as the yearly differences of the seasons and the winds—of which the sun is for the most part the cause—while those that are less so are known by men already habituated of necessity to observation, as sailors know the particular signs of storms and winds, which occur more periodically through the configurations of the moon, or of the fixed stars too, in relation to the sun. Yet because they cannot, through inexperience, accurately discern either the times and places of these very signs, or the periods of the wandering stars—which also contribute very much—it comes about that they often go astray. What, then, prevents one who has accurately learned the motions of all the stars, and of the sun and moon, so that neither the place nor the time of any of their configurations escapes him; and who has further discerned, from continuous inquiry handed down from of old, their natures for the most part—if not those in their actual subject, at least their natures as potentially productive (as that of the sun, that it warms; that of the moon, that it moistens; and so on with the rest); and who is competent, faced with such things, to determine the proper quality of the mixture both naturally and well-aimed from the combination of all—what prevents such a man from being able, at each of the given times, to state from the disposition of the phenomena then prevailing the proper characters of the surrounding heavens, as that it will be hotter or moister; and likewise, in the case of each individual man, to perceive the general quality of his temperament from the heavens prevailing at his constitution, as that he is such in body and such in soul, and to foretell his occasional accidents, by reasoning that such-and-such a state of the surrounding heavens is commensurate, and even suited, to such-and-such a temperament for good health, while such another is incommensurate and suited to harm? But that this apprehension is possible may be understood from these and the like considerations.

That with plausibility, but not with justice, it has incurred the charge of impossibility we may understand as follows. First, the mistakes of those who do not practise the art accurately, being many—as in a great study with many parts—have lent to its very truths the opinion of being due to chance, and this not rightly; for such a thing is not a weakness of the science, but of those who handle it. Next, the greater number, for the sake of gain, dignify another art with the name of this one, and so deceive the unlearned, seeming to foretell many things, even of those which have no nature to be foreknown; and by this they have given the more inquisitive an occasion to condemn even the foretelling of things that do have a nature to be foretold—and this not fittingly either. For philosophy is not to be abolished because some who profess it are revealed as base. Nevertheless it is plain that even if one approaches these studies as inquiringly and as genuinely as possible, he may often go wrong, not through any of the causes mentioned, but through the very nature of the matter and the weakness of his powers against the greatness of the profession. For, in general, besides the fact that all study concerning the quality of matter is conjectural and not capable of firm assertion—especially that compounded from many unlike things—there is the further point that the ancient configurations of the wandering stars, from which we apply to those which now stand in like positions the predictions observed by our predecessors in those former cases, can be more or less similar, yet by no means identical, since the exact return of all things in the heaven together with the earth either is never completed at all, or at least is not completed within a time perceptible to man—unless one wishes to indulge a vain conceit about the apprehension and knowledge of things that cannot be apprehended. Hence, the underlying patterns being unlike, the predictions sometimes fail. Concerning the examination of the events that occur in the surrounding heavens, then, this alone would be the difficulty, no cause being there taken into account besides the motion of the heavenly bodies. But concerning matters of nativities, and in general the particular constitution of each individual, one may see that there are causes neither small nor trifling which themselves cooperate in producing the proper character of the things constituted. For the differences of the seeds have very great power toward the special quality of the kind; since, the surrounding heavens and the horizon being the same, each of the seeds prevails to its own general form, as of man, of horse, and the rest. And the places of birth bring about no small variations in the things constituted: for the seeds being the same in kind—human, say—and the state of the surrounding heavens being the same, those born differ greatly, by reason of the difference of countries, both in their bodies and in their souls. Besides these, the modes of nurture and the customs, all the foregoing being supposed indifferent, contribute something to the particular ways of men's lives. Unless each of these is taken into account together with the causes from the surrounding heavens—even though this last has by far the greatest power, since the surrounding heavens is a cause that they too should be of such a kind, while they are in no way a cause to it—they can cause great perplexity to those who suppose, in such cases, that everything, even what does not depend wholly on the heavens, can be discerned from the motion of the heavenly bodies alone.

This being so, it would be fitting neither, because such prediction can sometimes fail, to do away with the whole of it—just as we do not reject navigation because it often fails—but rather, as in matters great and divine, to welcome the possible and count it a thing to be cherished; nor again to demand of it everything in a human and conjectural way, but to share in the love of the noble work, and where the whole did not depend on it, to supply the rest. And just as with physicians, when they make inquiry into the disease itself and into the particular character of the patient, we do not blame them for speaking, so here we should not be vexed at those who lay down the kinds and the countries and the modes of nurture, or any of the things that have already befallen.
On the characteristics of whole climes

Of the national characteristics, then, some are divided by whole parallels and whole quadrants, by their relation to the circle through the middle of the signs and to the sun. For since our inhabited world lies in one of the northern quadrants, those who live under the more southern parallels—I mean those from the equator to the summer tropic—have the sun overhead and are scorched, and so are black in body, with hair that is woolly and thick, of contracted form and stunted in size, hot in their natures and for the most part wild in their manners, on account of the unbroken heat of their dwellings. These we commonly call the Ethiopians. And not only do we see the men so disposed, but the surrounding condition of their air, and the other animals and the plants among them, display the same burning.

Those under the more northern parallels—I mean those who live under the Bears and have that region overhead—being far removed from the zodiac and from the heat of the sun, are for this reason cooled; but, partaking more abundantly of moist substance, which is most nourishing and is drawn up by no heat, they are white in color and straight-haired, large of body and well-grown in size, and somewhat cold in their natures; and they too are wild in their manners, on account of the unbroken cold of their dwellings. To these correspond the wintriness of the air that surrounds them, the great size of the plants, and the savageness of the animals. These too we generally call the Scythians.

Those between the summer tropic and the Bears, since the sun is neither overhead among them nor far removed at its meridian passages, share in the good temperature of the air—though this varies, it does not take a very great difference between heats and colds. Hence they are intermediate in color, moderate in size, well-tempered in their natures, settled in their dwellings, and gentle in their manners. Of these, those toward the south are, generally speaking, more keen of wit and inventive, and more competent in the inquiry into things divine, because the region overhead among them lies nearer the zodiac and the wandering stars about it; with which they have, fittingly, movements of soul that are quick to attain and searching, and given to traversing what are properly called the mathematical sciences. And of these again, those toward the east are more masculine and vigorous of soul and reveal all things openly, since one would reasonably suppose the risings to be of the solar nature, and that region to be diurnal and masculine and on the right—just as among living creatures we see that the right-hand parts are more apt for strength and vigor. But those toward the west are more feminine and softer of soul, and conceal most things, since this region in turn is of the moon, the moon always making her first appearances and her phases after conjunction from the west. For this reason the western clime seems nocturnal, feminine, and on the left, opposite to the eastern.

Already, too, in each of these whole parts there have followed by nature certain characteristic circumstances of manners and customs. For just as, in the conditions of the surrounding heavens, even among the regions reckoned generally as hot or cold or well-tempered, particular places and countries are distinguished in a greater or lesser degree—whether by the disposition of their situation, or by height, or by lowness, or by juxtaposition; and again, just as some are more given to horsemanship through the level character of the country, some to seafaring through the nearness of the sea, and some are gentle through the abundance of the land—so too, from the natural kinship of the particular climes with the stars according to the signs, one would find characteristic natures among each people; and these too generally rather than as present in every single individual without exception. It is necessary, then, in the cases where it may be useful for the particular examinations, to go through them summarily.
On the horoscopic degree

Since concerning the first and most authoritative thing—that is, the degree of the hour at the bringing-forth—there is often a difficulty, only the inspection through astrolabe horoscopic instruments at the very birth being generally able to suggest the precise part of the hour to those who observe scientifically, while almost all the other horoscopic instruments, to which most of the more careful give their attention, are able in many ways to depart from the truth: the solar ones from the distortions of their positions and gnomons that occur, and the water-clocks from the stoppages and irregularities in the flow of the water, brought about by various causes and by chance—it would be necessary to set forth beforehand by what manner one may find the degree of the zodiac that ought to be rising according to the natural and consistent method, when the degree found by the practice of the risings, according to the approximate hour given, has been laid down beforehand. One must then take the conjunction last preceding the bringing-forth, whether it be a new moon or a full moon, and, having examined the degree accurately—in the case of a new moon, that of both lights, in the case of a full moon, that of the one of them above the earth—at the time of the bringing-forth see which of the stars have a ruling relation to it, the manner of rulership being observed generally in these five: triangle, house, exaltation, term, and phase or configuration; that is, whenever the place sought has one or more of these, or also all, toward the one that is to rule. If, then, we find one star fittingly disposed toward all these, or the most of them, whatever degree this star precisely occupies in the sign through which it is passing, at the time of the bringing-forth we shall judge that the degree equal in number to it is rising in the nearest sign found by the practice of the risings. But if there be two or more jointly ruling, that one whose degree-passage at the bringing-forth has its number nearer to the rising degree according to the risings—of his amount of degrees we shall make use. And if two or more be near in number, we shall follow the one having more relation both to the angles and to the sect. If, however, the distance of the ruling degrees be greater toward the more comprehensive horoscope than toward the similar midheaven, having made use of the same number toward the culminating degree, through this we shall set out also the remaining angles.
Concerning acquisitive fortune

What the nature of a person's possessions will be must be taken from what is called the Lot of Fortune — but only from this one Lot, by which we always project the distance from the Sun to the Moon, measuring it from the Ascendant for those born by day as well as for those born by night, for the reasons we gave in our discussion of the times of life. When it has been established in this way, one must observe by taking the rulership of the twelfth-part in which it falls, and noting how these rulers stand in power and in familiarity, in the manner we defined at the outset; and further the planets that are configured with them or that dominate them, whether of the same or of the contrary sect. For when those that have taken the rulership of the Lot are powerful, they make men wealthy in possessions, and especially when they happen to be properly attested by the luminaries. But Saturn does this through buildings or agriculture or shipping; Jupiter through trusteeship or guardianships or priesthoods; Mars through military service and commands; Venus through gifts from friends or women; Mercury through eloquence and trade. And in particular, Saturn, when allied to acquisitive fortune, if he is configured with Jupiter, brings about inheritances, and especially when this occurs at the upper angles, with Jupiter in a bicorporeal sign or holding the application of the Moon; for then men are also adopted into another's family and inherit the estates of strangers. And if the planets of the same sect as the rulers happen themselves to bear witness to the rulerships, they preserve possessions undiminished; but if those of the contrary sect dominate the governing places or rise after them, they bring about the loss of one's holdings, the general time of this being taken from the inclination of the planets that produce the cause toward the angles and the places that rise after them.
That it is also useful

In what manner, then, prediction through astronomy becomes possible, and that it can reach only as far as the events occurring in the surrounding heavens themselves and what befalls men from that cause—these being matters concerning the original aptitudes of the powers and actions of body and soul, and their occasional affections, their length or shortness of life, and further whatever among external things has an authoritative and natural connection with the primary ones (as, for the body, possessions and cohabitation; for the soul, honour and dignity), together with their occasional fortunes—nearly all this has been made plain to us as in summary. It would remain to make in brief the examination concerning what is useful, first determining in what manner, and toward what end, we shall understand the very power of the useful. For if it be toward the goods of the soul, what could be more conducive to well-being, joy, and altogether contentment than such foreknowledge, by which we become observers of things both human and divine? And if toward the goods of the body, such apprehension, more than anything, would recognize what is proper and suited to the aptitude of each temperament. And if it does not cooperate toward wealth, or fame, or such things, then the same may be said of all philosophy; for of none of these things is it, of itself, productive. Yet we should not on this account justly condemn either philosophy or this art, putting aside the benefit they bring toward greater things.

In general, on examination, those who blame the apprehension as useless would appear to look toward none of the most important things, but only to this one—that the foreknowledge of things that will in any case come to pass is superfluous; and this, too, said quite simply and without good distinction. For first we must observe that even in things which will of necessity come about, the unexpected most naturally produces panic that drives men out of their senses, and joys that carry them away; whereas foreknowledge accustoms and orders the soul by the practice of regarding things absent as present, and prepares it to receive each of the things that come with peace and steadiness. Next, that we should not even so suppose that each thing follows for men from the cause above, as though from the beginning it were ordained for every single one by some indissoluble and divine command, and would of necessity come to pass, no other cause being at all able to work against it; but rather thus: that the motion of the heavenly bodies is accomplished from eternity in accordance with a divine and unalterable destiny, while the alteration of earthly things takes its first causes from above by accident and consequence, in accordance with a destiny that is natural and changeable. And further, that some things befall men through more universal circumstances, and not from each man's own natural aptitude—as when, through great and unguardable changes of the surrounding heavens, multitudes perish together by fires or plagues or floods, the lesser cause always yielding to the greater and stronger—while others befall through each man's own natural temperament, by reason of small and chance contrary influences of the surrounding heavens. For these things being thus distinguished, it is plain that, both universally and in particular, of whatever events the first cause is irresistible and greater than anything opposing it, these must in any case come to pass; but of whatever are not so, those that meet with the contrary influences are easily turned aside, while those that do not find them follow likewise the primary natures—through ignorance, however, and no longer through the necessity of strength. One may see the same thing happening also in all things simply that have natural beginnings. For of stones and plants and animals, and further of wounds and affections and diseases, some by nature do something of necessity, others only if nothing of the contrary works against them. So, then, we must suppose that the scientific men also foretell what will befall men by such foreknowledge, and approach it not according to empty opinions—holding that of some things, because their productive causes are many and great, men are unguarded, while others admit of changes through the opposite cause. Just as among physicians those who are able to read the symptoms foreknow both what is altogether fatal and what admits of help. And concerning things that can be changed, the astrologer is to be heard in this way: that, when the underlying proportions of such-and-such a temperament have been turned, by such-and-such a character of the surrounding heavens, to the more or the less, such-and-such an affection will follow—just as the physician says that this ulcer will spread or fester, and the miner, for example, that the magnet stone attracts iron. For as each of these, if left alone through ignorance of the contrary influences, will in every way follow the power of its primary nature—yet the ulcer will work neither the spreading nor the festering should it meet with the opposing treatment, nor will the magnet draw the iron if garlic be rubbed upon it (and these very hindrances too worked their counter-effect naturally and by destiny)—so too in those other cases: things that will befall men, if unknown, or even if known yet not meeting with the contrary influences, will in every way follow the chain of the primary nature; but if foreknown and provided with the remedies, they are set right again naturally and by destiny, becoming either wholly unrealized or more moderate. And since, in general, such power is the same both in things viewed comprehensively and in particular matters, one might wonder for what cause it is that, in universal matters, all men believe both in the possibility of foreknowledge and in its usefulness for taking precaution—for most men acknowledge that they foreknow the seasons, the signs of the fixed stars, and the configurations of the moon, and they take much forethought for guarding against them, always providing, against summer, things able to cool, and against winter, things that warm, and in general preparing their own natures toward an even balance; and again, for the safety of their seasons and their voyages, watching the signs of the fixed stars, and for the beginnings of mating and planting, the configurations occurring at the filling of the moon's lights—and no one anywhere has ever condemned such things as impossible or useless; whereas in particular matters, and as regards the special qualities arising from the temperament of the rest—such as more and less of cold, or even of heat, and each man's own temperament—some hold that foreknowledge is no longer possible, nor that one can in most cases guard against them; although it is quite plain that, if we have cooled ourselves beforehand against general heat-waves we shall be less scorched, and the same may avail against what particularly raises the heat of a given temperament to excess. But the cause of such error is the difficulty and unfamiliarity of foreknowledge in particular matters, which produces distrust in nearly all the rest as well. And because the power that works against the predictive power is for the most part not joined to it—through the rarity of so perfect a disposition, and because matters are accomplished about the primary natures without hindrance—this has produced the opinion that everything that will come to pass is unalterable and unguardable.

But just as, I think, in the case of prognosis itself, even if it were not throughout infallible, yet its possibility appeared worthy of the greatest zeal, in the same way in the case of the protective power too: even if it does not heal all things, but only some, and these few and small, we should still love and welcome it and count it no ordinary gain. The Egyptians, who advanced this power of the art most of all, seem to have recognized this, and so everywhere joined medicine to prediction through astronomy. For they would never have set up certain modes of averting, and amulets, and remedies against the circumstances coming or present from the surrounding heavens, both universal and particular, had they held any opinion of the immobility and unchangeableness of things to come. But, placing the power that can work against the subsequent natures in second rank to the doctrine of destiny, they joined to the power of foreknowledge what is useful and beneficial, by means of what they call among themselves the works of iatromathematics—so that through astronomy they might come to know the qualities of the underlying temperaments, and the events that would arise through the surrounding heavens, and their proper causes (since, without knowledge of these, the remedies too must for the most part fail, as not all bodies or affections answer to the same applications); and that through medicine, from the things that are by sympathy proper or contrary to each, they might continually make, as far as possible, both the precautions against affections to come and the cures of those present, without failure.

But let these things be sketched for us thus far in summary. We shall now make our discourse in the manner of an introduction, beginning with the proper character of each of the heavenly bodies as to its very productive power, following the observations applied by the ancients in the natural manner; and first with the powers of the wandering stars, and of the sun and moon.
On the kinship of countries with the triangles and the stars

There are four triangular figures observed in the zodiac, as has been shown by us in what precedes. That which is by the Ram, the Lion, and the Archer is north-and-southwestern, and is ruled chiefly by Jupiter on account of the north, and jointly by Mars on account of the southwest. That by the Bull, the Virgin, and the Goat-horned is south-and-eastern, and is ruled again chiefly by Venus on account of the south, and jointly by Saturn on account of the east. That by the Twins, the Claws, and the Water-pourer is north-and-eastern, and is ruled chiefly by Saturn on account of the east, and jointly by Jupiter on account of the north. That by the Crab, the Scorpion, and the Fishes is south-and-southwestern, and is ruled chiefly by Mars on account of the southwest, and jointly by Venus on account of the south.

This being so, and our inhabited world being divided into four quadrants, equal in number to the triangles—in breadth by our sea, from the strait of Heracles to the gulf of Issus and the mountain ridge that follows it eastward, by which its southern and its northern parts are separated; and in length by the Arabian gulf, and by the Aegean Sea, the Pontus, and the Maeotic Lake, by which its eastern and southwestern parts are separated—there come to be four quadrants, agreeing with the position of the triangles. One lies toward the northwest of the whole inhabited world, that about Celtic Gaul, which we commonly call Europe; opposite to it, toward the south-east, is that about eastern Ethiopia, which would be called the southern part of greater Asia. Again, that toward the north-east of the whole inhabited world is that about Scythia, which is itself the northern part of greater Asia; and opposite to it, toward the south-southwest wind, is that about western Ethiopia, which we commonly call Libya.

Again, of each of the foregoing quadrants, the parts disposed more toward the middle of the whole inhabited world take a position contrary to that of the encompassing quadrant, as that quadrant does toward the whole inhabited world. The quadrant about Europe lies toward the northwest of the whole inhabited world, yet the parts about its middle, and the opposite-cornered, are seen to hold a position toward the south-east of that same quadrant. And so likewise with the others; so that from these each of the quadrants is made kindred to two opposite triangles: the other parts of it being fitted to its general inclination, while the parts about the middle are taken up, for the kinship, with the triangle opposite to that of its own quadrant. And of the stars that hold the rulership in their proper triangles, in the other dwellings those alone again rule, while in the parts about the middle of the inhabited world those rule, and further Mercury also, on account of his being in the middle and common to the sects.

From such an arrangement, then, the other parts of the first quadrant—I mean that about Europe—lying toward the northwest of the whole inhabited world, are made kindred to the north-and-southwestern triangle, that by the Ram, the Lion, and the Archer, and are ruled, as is fitting, by the lords of the triangle, Jupiter and Mars, in their western station. These countries, taken by whole nations, are Britain, Gaul, Germany, Bastarnia, Italy, Gallia, Apulia, Sicily, Tyrrhenia, the Celtic land, and Spain. It befell the aforesaid nations, generally speaking—both through the leading character of the triangle and through the jointly ruling stars—to be unsubdued, lovers of freedom, lovers of arms, lovers of toil, most warlike, fitted for command, clean, and great-souled. Yet through the western station of Jupiter and Mars, and further through the fact that the foremost parts of the said triangle are masculine and the hinder feminine, it befell them to be indifferent toward women and contemptuous of the pleasures of love, but more sated with intercourse with males and more jealous of it; and those who submit to such usage do not reckon what is done shameful, nor do they become on this account truly unmanly and soft, since they are not affected passively, but keep their souls manly, sociable, faithful, friendly to their own, and beneficent. And of these countries themselves, Britain, Gaul, Germany, and Bastarnia are more kindred to the Ram and to Mars; whence those in them are generally wilder, more headstrong, and beast-like. Italy and Apulia, Gallia and Sicily are kindred to the Lion and to the sun; wherefore these are more fit for command, beneficent, and sociable. Tyrrhenia, the Celtic land, and Spain are kindred to the Archer and to Jupiter; whence comes their love of freedom, their simplicity, and their love of cleanliness.

The parts within this quadrant disposed about the middle of the inhabited world—Thrace, Macedonia, Illyria, Hellas, Achaea, Crete, and further the Cyclades and the coastlands of Asia Minor and of Cyprus—lying toward the south-east of the whole quadrant, take on in addition the kinship of the south-and-eastern triangle, that by the Bull, the Virgin, and the Goat-horned, and as joint rulers Venus, Saturn, and Mercury; whence those who inhabit these countries turned out more balanced and blended both in body and in soul. Being themselves fit for command, noble, and unsubdued through Mars; lovers of freedom and self-governing and democratic and lawgiving through Jupiter; lovers of the Muses and of learning, contentious and clean in their diet through Venus; sociable, hospitable, lovers of justice, lovers of letters, and most effective in discourse through Mercury; and most given to the performance of mysteries through the western station of Venus. And again, by particular regions, those about the Cyclades and the coastlands of Asia Minor and of Cyprus are more kindred to the Bull and to Venus; whence for the most part they are luxurious, clean, and given to care of the body. Those about Hellas, Achaea, and Crete are kindred to the Virgin and to Mercury; wherefore they are more rational and lovers of learning, and exercise the things of the soul before those of the body. Those about Macedonia, Thrace, and Illyria are kindred to the Goat-horned and to Saturn; wherefore they are lovers of possessions, but not so gentle, nor sociable in their laws.

Of the second quadrant, that by the southern part of greater Asia: its other parts, comprising India, Ariana, Gedrosia, Parthia, Media, Persis, Babylonia, Mesopotamia, and Assyria, and holding their position toward the south-east of the whole inhabited world, are reasonably made kindred to the south-and-eastern triangle of the Bull, the Virgin, and the Goat-horned, and are ruled by Venus and Saturn in their eastern stations. Wherefore one would find the natures of those in them following accordingly upon what is accomplished by stars that so rule. For they revere Venus, naming her Isis, and Saturn, naming him Mithras the Sun; and most of them foretell things to come. Among them, too, the generative parts are consecrated, on account of the seedlike conformation of the said stars, which is by nature generative. Further, they are hot, lustful, and prone to the pleasures of love; given to dancing and leaping and to adornment through Venus, and luxurious in life through Saturn. They conduct their intercourse with women openly and not in secret, on account of the eastern character of the configuration, but they greatly abhor intercourse with males. For these reasons it befell most of them to beget children of their own mothers, and to make their obeisances with the breast, on account of the eastern risings and the fact that the rule of the heart is fittingly disposed toward the solar power. They are, generally, in other respects—in dress and adornment and bodily habits altogether—delicate and effeminate through Venus, but in soul and purpose great-minded, noble, and warlike, through Saturn's being fittingly disposed toward the figure of the risings. By particular regions, again, Parthia, Media, and Persis are more kindred to the Bull and to Venus; whence those there use flowered garments, covering themselves wholly except the breast, and are altogether luxurious and clean. To the Virgin and to Mercury belong the parts about Babylon, Mesopotamia, and Assyria; wherefore among those there the mathematical art and the observation of the five stars came to be preeminent. To the Goat-horned and to Saturn belong the parts about India, Ariana, and Gedrosia; whence the shapelessness, uncleanness, and beast-likeness of those who dwell in those countries. The remaining parts of the quadrant, disposed about the middle of the whole inhabited world—Idumaea, Coele-Syria, Judaea, Phoenicia, the Chaldean land, Orchenia, and Arabia the Blessed—holding their position toward the northwest of the whole quadrant, take on in addition the kinship of the north-and-southwestern triangle, of the Ram, the Lion, and the Archer, and further as joint rulers Jupiter, Mars, and Mercury; wherefore these are more given to commerce and exchange than the others, but more knavish, despicably cowardly, treacherous, slavish of soul, and altogether fickle, through the conformation of the said stars. And of these again, those about Coele-Syria, Idumaea, and Judaea are more kindred to the Ram and to Mars; wherefore for the most part they are bold, godless, and treacherous. The Phoenicians, Chaldeans, and Orchenians are kindred to the Lion and to the sun, wherefore they are simpler, humane, lovers of astrology, and of all men the greatest worshippers of the sun. Those of Arabia the Blessed are kindred to the Archer and to Jupiter; whence, accordingly with its name, came the fertility of the country, the abundance of spices, and the fitness of the people for a free manner of life, for exchange, and for commerce.

Of the third quadrant, that by the northern part of greater Asia: its other parts, comprising Hyrcania, Armenia, Matiana, Bactriana, Casperia, Serica, Sauromatica, Oxiana, and Sogdiana, lying toward the north-east of the whole inhabited world, are made kindred to the north-and-eastern triangle of the Twins, the Scales, and the Water-pourer, and are ruled, as is fitting, by Saturn and Jupiter in their eastern figures. Wherefore those who hold these countries revere Jupiter and Saturn, are most wealthy and full of gold, clean in their diet and elegant in their way of life, wise in things divine, magi, just in their manners, free, great and noble of soul, haters of wickedness and tender in affection, ready to die for their nearest for the sake of what is noble and holy; dignified and clean in their use of the pleasures of love, lavish in dress, generous and great-minded—all of which, generally speaking, the eastern conformation of Saturn and Jupiter brings about. And of these nations again, the parts about Hyrcania, Armenia, and Matiana are more kindred to the Twins and to Mercury; wherefore they are more nimble and somewhat knavish. The parts about Bactriana, Casperia, and Serica are kindred to the Scales and to Venus; whence those who possess these countries are most wealthy, lovers of the Muses, and more luxurious. The parts about Sauromatica, Oxiana, and Sogdiana are kindred to the Water-pourer and to Saturn; wherefore these nations too are more savage, austere, and beast-like. The remaining parts of this quadrant, lying about the middle of the whole inhabited world—Bithynia, Phrygia, Colchica, Syria, Commagene, Cappadocia, Lydia, Lycia, Cilicia, and Pamphylia—holding their position toward the south-southwest of the quadrant itself, take on in addition the kinship of the south-and-southwestern quadrant of the Crab, the Scorpion, and the Fishes, and as joint rulers Mars, Venus, and Mercury; wherefore those about these countries generally revere Venus as the mother of the gods, addressing her by various local names, and Mars as Adonis or by some other name again, and render to them certain mysteries with lamentations. They are exceedingly wretched and slavish of soul, laborious, wicked, given to mercenary service, plunder, and captivity, enslaving themselves and falling into ruin by wars. And through Mars and Venus in their eastern conjunction—because in the Goat-horned, the triangular sign of Venus, Mars is exalted, while in the Fishes, the triangular sign of Mars, Venus is exalted—it came about that the women show all goodwill toward their husbands, being tender in affection, keepers of the house, industrious, serviceable, and altogether laborious and submissive. And of these again, those about Bithynia, Phrygia, and Colchica are more kindred to the Crab and to the moon; wherefore the men generally are cautious and submissive, while most of the women, through the eastern and masculinized figure of the moon, are manly, fit for rule, and warlike, like the Amazons—shunning intercourse with men, lovers of arms, and masculinizing all female children from infancy by cutting off the right breasts for the sake of soldierly needs, and laying bare these parts in their array, to display the unfeminine character of their nature. Those about Syria, Commagene, and Cappadocia are kindred to the Scorpion and to Mars; wherefore among them there is much boldness, wickedness, treachery, and toil. Those about Lydia, Cilicia, and Pamphylia are kindred to the Fishes and to Jupiter; whence these are more possessing of property, given to commerce, sociable, free, and faithful in their dealings.

Of the remaining quadrant, that about what is commonly called Libya: its other parts, comprising Numidia, Carthaginia, Africa, Phazania, Nasamonitis, Garamantica, Mauritania, Gaetulia, and Metagonitis, holding their position toward the south-southwest of the whole inhabited world, are made kindred to the south-and-southwestern triangle of the Crab, the Scorpion, and the Fishes, and are ruled, as is fitting, by Mars and Venus in their western figure. Wherefore it befell most of them, on account of the said conjunction of the stars, to be ruled by a man and a woman, brother and sister of the same mother—the man ruling the men, the woman the women—and such succession being maintained. They are exceedingly hot and prone to intercourse with women, so that they even make their marriages by seizure, and in many places the kings are first to lie with the brides; and among some the women are common to all. They are lovers of finery, and gird on women's adornments, through Venus; yet manly in soul, somewhat knavish, and given to magic; and counterfeiters, reckless, and headstrong through Mars. And of these again, those about Numidia, Carthage, and Africa are more kindred to the Crab and to the moon; wherefore these are sociable, given to commerce, and pass their lives in all abundance. Those about Metagonitis, Mauritania, and Gaetulia are kindred to the Scorpion and to Mars; whence these are more beast-like, most warlike, eaters of flesh, exceedingly reckless, and contemptuous of life, so that they do not even spare one another. Those about Phazania, Nasamonitis, and Garamantica are kindred to the Fishes and to Jupiter; wherefore they are free, simple in manners, lovers of work, fair-minded, clean, and generally unsubdued, and they worship Jupiter as Ammon. The remaining parts of the quadrant, disposed toward the middle of the whole inhabited world—Cyrenaica, Marmarica, Egypt, the Thebaid, the Oasis, the Troglodyte land, Arabia, Azania, and central Ethiopia—turned toward the north-east of the whole quadrant, take on in addition the kinship of the north-and-eastern triangle of the Twins, the Scales, and the Water-pourer, and on this account as joint rulers Saturn, Jupiter, and further Mercury. Whence those throughout these countries, having shared in the western rulership of nearly the five planets, have become lovers of the gods, god-fearing, devoted to the divine, lovers of lamentation, and burying and hiding their dead in the earth on account of the western figure; using all manner of customs and usages and worships of all manner of gods. In subjection they are humble, timid, mean-spirited, and patient of toil; in command, high of spirit and great-minded. They take many wives and many husbands, are prone to lust, and unite with their sisters; and the men are prolific in seed, the women easily conceiving, in keeping with the fruitfulness of the country. Many of the males, too, are unsound and effeminate in soul, and some hold even the generative parts in contempt, through the western conformation of the maleficent stars together with Venus. And of these, those about Cyrenaica and Marmarica, and especially those about lower Egypt, are more kindred to the Twins and to Mercury; wherefore these are thoughtful and intelligent and quick to attain in all things, and especially in the discovery of things wise and divine; given to magic, performers of hidden mysteries, and altogether competent in the mathematical sciences. Those about the Thebaid, the Oasis, and the Troglodyte land are kindred to the Scales and to Venus; whence these too are hotter in their natures, more lively, and pass their lives in fruitfulness. Those about Arabia, Azania, and central Ethiopia are kindred to the Water-pourer and to Saturn; wherefore these too are eaters of flesh and eaters of fish, and are nomads, living a wild and beast-like life.

The kinships, then, of the stars and the signs with the several nations, and their characteristics in general, have been sketched by us in this summary fashion. And for the convenience of use, we shall set out, under each of the signs, by bare juxtaposition, the several nations kindred to it, in keeping with what has been said of them before, in this manner.
Ram: Britain, Gaul, Germany, Bastarnia; about the middle, Coele-Syria, Palestine, Idumaea, Judaea.
Bull: Parthia, Media, Persis; about the middle, the Cyclades islands, Cyprus, the coastlands of Asia Minor.
Twins: Hyrcania, Armenia, Matiana; about the middle, Cyrenaica, Marmarica, lower Egypt.
Crab: Numidia, Carthaginia, Africa; about the middle, Bithynia, Phrygia, Colchica.
Lion: Italy, Gallia, Sicily, Apulia; about the middle, Phoenicia, Chaldea, Orchenia.
Virgin: Mesopotamia, Babylonia, Assyria; about the middle, Hellas, Achaea, Crete.
Scales: Bactriana, Casperia, Serica; about the middle, the Thebaid, the Oasis, the Troglodyte land.
Scorpion: Metagonitis, Mauritania, Gaetulia; about the middle, Syria, Commagene, Cappadocia.
Archer: Tyrrhenia, the Celtic land, Spain; about the middle, Arabia the Blessed.
Goat-horned: India, Ariana, Gedrosia; about the middle, Thrace, Macedonia, Illyria.
Water-pourer: Sauromatica, Oxiana, Sogdiana; about the middle, Arabia, Azania, central Ethiopia.
Fishes: Phazania, Nasamonitis, Garamantica; about the middle, Lydia, Cilicia, Pamphylia.

These being set out, it is reasonable to add this too to the present part: that each of the fixed stars also is kindred to as many countries as the parts of the zodiac with which the fixed stars share their inclinations on the circle drawn through its poles are seen to make their sympathy; and that, in the case of metropolises, those places of the zodiac are most in sympathy through which the sun and moon happened to be passing, as at a nativity, at the inceptions of their foundings, and especially the horoscopic point of the angles; and where the times of the foundings are not found, the places upon which falls the midheaven in the nativities of those who at the time were rulers or kings.
The division of genethlialogy

These things having been set out beforehand, if one should, for the sake of order itself, divide the whole of genethlialogical theory, he would find that, of the apprehensions that are according to nature and possible, one is of events before the birth only, as the account concerning parents; another of events both before the birth and after the birth, as the account concerning brothers and sisters; another of events at the very birth, no longer so single and simple; and last of events after the birth, this too observed as more manifold. Of the things sought at the very birth are the account concerning males and females, the account concerning twins or multiple births, the account concerning monstrous births, and the account concerning those not reared. Of the things after the birth: the account concerning the length of life, since it is not joined to that concerning those not reared; then the account concerning the form of the body and the account concerning bodily sufferings or injuries; next the account concerning the quality of the soul and the account concerning sufferings of the soul; then the account concerning the fortune of possessions and the account concerning the fortune of dignity; and after these the account concerning the quality of action; then the account concerning the partnership of marriage, the account concerning the begetting of children, and the account concerning unions and friends; next the account concerning travel abroad; and last the account concerning the quality of death, which in power is kindred to that concerning the length of life, but in order is reasonably set after all these. Concerning each of these we shall make our exposition in summary, setting out the very practices of the examination together with the bare productive powers, as we said; sending away the things that are foolishly babbled over by the many, having no plausible relation to the causes from the first nature; but examining the things that admit of apprehension, not through lots and numbers without cause assigned, but through the very theory of the configurations toward the proper places—generally, however, and over all simply, that we may not repeat ourselves with each kind.

First one must consider the place of the zodiac made proper to the kind of birth sought under each heading—as, for example, the midheaven for that concerning actions, or the solar place for that concerning the father; then observe the stars that have a relation to the underlying place, according to the five modes of rulership we set out above. And if there be one lord according to all of them, to him is to be given the rulership of that prediction; but if two or three, to those that have the more votes. After this, for the quality of the event, one must consider the natures both of the ruling stars themselves and of the signs in which they and the kindred places are; and for the magnitude of the event, one must consider also their power—whether they happen to be effectively disposed both cosmically and at the birth, or the contrary. For they are most active when, cosmically, they are in their own or familiar places, and again when they happen to be eastern and additive in their numbers; and at the birth, when they pass over the angles or the post-ascensions, and especially the first ones—I mean those at the risings and the culminations. They are most feeble when, cosmically, they are in alien or unfamiliar places, and are western or retrograde in their courses; and at the birth, when they decline from the angles. And for the general time of the event, one must consider whether they are eastern or western with respect to the sun and to the horoscope—since the leading quadrants of each of these, and their diameters, are eastern, while the remaining and following ones are western—and whether they happen to be upon the angles or the post-ascensions; for being eastern or at an angle they become more active at the beginning, but being western or upon the post-ascensions, slower.
Concerning dignitary fortune

The matters of rank and of this kind of good fortune must be examined from the disposition of the luminaries and from the familiarity of the attending planets to them. For when both luminaries are in masculine signs, and when either both again or even one of them are at an angle — especially the one of the sect — and when it is attended by the five planets (the Sun by morning stars, the Moon by evening stars), those born will be kings. And if the attending planets are themselves at an angle, or are configured with the angle above the earth, the natives continue great and powerful and rulers of the world; and they are still more fortunate if the attending planets are configured to the right of the angles above the earth. But if, while the other conditions hold, the Sun alone is in a masculine sign and the Moon in a feminine one, but one of the luminaries is at an angle, they will only be leaders, masters of life and death. And if, besides this, the attending planets are not at an angle and do not bear witness to the angles, they will only be great men, in dignities that are partial — bearers of crowns, or procurators, or commanders of camps — but not in the highest commands. But if the luminaries are not at an angle, while most of the attending planets either are at an angle or are configured with the angles, men will not attain conspicuous dignities, but will rise in civic offices and reach a moderate standing in their pursuits in life. If, however, none of the attending planets is allied to the angles, they remain obscure in their undertakings and without advancement. And they become utterly humble and ill-fated in their fortunes whenever neither of the luminaries is at an angle, nor falls in a masculine sign, nor is attended by the benefics. Such, then, is the general outline of the examination set before us, and such is the increase and decrease of dignities. But the conditions that lie between these, which are very numerous, must be conjectured from the particular variation in the form of the luminaries themselves and of their attendance, and from the predominance among the attendants. For when this attendance belongs to the planets of the sect or to the benefics, the dignities are more genuinely and more securely held; but when it belongs to the opposing planets or to the malefics, they are more subordinate and more precarious. And the form of the dignity that is to be must be considered from the particular nature of the attending planets. For Saturn, when he holds the chief place in the attendance, makes the powers rest on abundance of possessions and the gathering of wealth; Jupiter or Venus, on favors and gifts and honors and acts of generosity; Mars, on campaigns and victories and the fear of subjects; Mercury, through intelligence or education and care and management of affairs.
On the power of the wandering stars

The sun has been apprehended as having the productive part of its substance in heating, and mildly in drying. These effects are more perceptible to us than the others, both because of its magnitude and because of the plainness of the changes in the seasons; for the nearer it comes to the point overhead us, the more it disposes us in this way. The moon has the greater part of her power in moistening, plainly because of her nearness to the earth and the exhalations from moist things; and she disposes bodies thus directly, ripening and chiefly causing decay, though she shares mildly also in heating, through the illumination from the sun.

The star of Saturn has the greater part of its quality in cooling and mildly in drying, because, as it seems, it is farthest removed at once from the heat of the sun and from the exhalations of the moist things about the earth. Powers are determined, both for this star and for the rest, also through the observation of their configurations to the sun and moon, since some appear to turn the state of the surrounding heavens, more or less, in one way, others in another.
The star of Mars has chiefly a nature of drying and burning, in keeping with its fiery colour and its nearness to the sun, beneath which lies the sun's own sphere.

The star of Jupiter has its productive power well-tempered, its motion lying midway between the cooling of Saturn and the burning of Mars. For it warms and at the same time moistens; and because it is more warming, owing to the spheres beneath it, it becomes productive of fertile winds.

The star of Venus is productive of the same well-tempered effects, but in the opposite way. For it warms mildly because of its nearness to the sun, but it moistens most of all, like the moon, both because of the greatness of its own lights and because it draws to itself the exhalation from the moist things surrounding the earth.

The star of Mercury is found for the most part to be, in equal measure, now drying and absorbing of moisture—because it is never far removed in longitude from the heat of the sun—and now again moistening, because it lies next to the sphere of the moon, which is nearest the earth; and it makes its changes in both directions quickly, being as it were driven by the winds through the swiftness of its motion about the sun itself.
Approach to particular predictions

These things having thus been examined beforehand, it would be consistent next to go through, in summary, the approaches to the predictions, and first of those taken with respect to whole countries or cities under general circumstances. The manner of examination will be of this kind. The first and strongest cause of such events arises in the eclipse-bearing conjunctions of sun and moon, and in the passages of the stars at those times. Of the prediction itself, one part is local, by which one must foreknow upon what countries or cities the particular eclipses, or also the seasonal fixed stations of the wandering stars, will fall—these being of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, when they make their stations; for they then produce their significations. Another part is temporal, by which one must foreknow the time of the significations and the amount of their duration. Another part is generic, by which it is fitting to grasp upon what kinds of things the event will fall. And last is the specific, by which we shall observe the quality of the very thing to be accomplished.
On parents

The leading type of the examination under each heading, which it is fitting to hold throughout, has this character. We shall now begin, according to the order set out, from the first, the account concerning parents. The sun, then, and the star of Saturn are made kindred by nature to the person of the father, the moon and the star of Venus to that of the mother; and however these may happen to be disposed, both toward one another and toward the others, such things must also be supposed concerning the parents. The things concerning their fortune and possessions are to be examined from the bodyguarding of the lights, since, when they are surrounded by stars able to do good and of the same sect—either in the same signs or also in the following—they signify that the affairs concerning the parents are conspicuous and brilliant, and most of all when eastern stars bodyguard the sun and western ones the moon, these themselves also being well disposed in the manner we have stated. And if both Saturn and Venus happen to be eastern and in their own persons, or also at the angles, manifest good fortune must be supposed, in keeping with what is proper to each of the parents. The contrary, if the lights are running their course empty and unguarded by bodyguards, is indicative of the lowliness and obscurity of the parents, and most of all when Venus or also Saturn appears ill-disposed. And if they be bodyguarded, but not by stars of the same sect—as when Mars rises after the sun, and Saturn after the moon—or not by well-placed benefic stars of the same sect, moderate fortune and unevenness about their life must be supposed. And if the Lot of Fortune that will be signified in the nativity agree with the stars that bodyguarded the sun or the moon for good, they will receive the property of the parents intact; but if it be discordant or contrary, no benefic having taken up the bodyguarding, or the malefics having done so, the property of the parents will be useless to them and harmful.

Concerning their length or shortness of life one must consider from the other configurations. For in the case of the father, if Jupiter or Venus be configured in any way with the sun and Saturn, or if Saturn himself have a harmonious configuration with the sun, whether conjunct or sextile or trine, they being in power, length of life of the father is to be conjectured; but if they be without power, not so, yet not shortness of life either. But if this be not so, and Mars overcome the sun or Saturn, or also rise after them, or if again Saturn himself be not harmonious toward the sun but either square or in diameter, then, when declining from the angles, they make the fathers merely sickly; but at the angles, or rising after the angles, they make them short-lived or injured—short-lived when they are in the first two angles, the rising and the culminating, and in their post-ascensions; injured or diseased when they are in the remaining two angles, the setting and the subterranean, or in their post-ascensions. For the star of Mars, beholding the sun in the manner we have stated, suddenly destroys the father, or produces injuries about the eyes; and beholding Saturn, brings him round to deaths or chills-and-fevers or injuries through cuttings and burnings. And the star of Saturn, himself also ill-configured toward the sun, contrives diseased deaths for the fathers, and sufferings through the trouble of the humors.

In the case of the mother, if Jupiter be configured with the moon and Venus in any way, or if Venus herself be harmoniously disposed toward the moon, being sextile or trine or conjunct, they being in power, they show the mother to be long-lived. But if Mars behold the moon, or Venus, having risen after them, or squared, or diametered them, or Saturn behold the moon alone likewise—they being subtractive or declining—again they bring round only mischances or weaknesses; but being additive or at the angles, they make the mothers short-lived or injured—short-lived likewise when they are at the eastern angles or post-ascensions, injured when at the western. For Mars, beholding the moon in this manner, she being eastern, makes the deaths of the mothers sudden and produces injuries about the eyes; but she being waning, deaths from miscarriages or such things, and the injuries through cuttings and burnings. And beholding Venus, he brings about feverish deaths and sufferings through hidden causes and dimmings and sudden onsets. And Saturn, beholding the moon, produces deaths and sufferings—she being eastern, through chills-and-fevers; but waning, through ulcerous corrosions of the womb and eatings-away.

One must take up in addition, for the particular kinds of injuries or sufferings or deaths, also the characteristics of the signs in which the stars producing the cause are, concerning which we shall work out more opportunely in the parts about the birth itself. And one must observe further, by day especially the sun and Venus, by night Saturn and the moon. It would remain, for the workings-out under each heading, to be fitting and consistent that, having set up the paternal or maternal place of the sect like a horoscope, we should examine the rest as at the nativity of the parents themselves, according to the approaches—to be shown next—of the more comprehensive kinds, both practical and incidental. Of the conjoint-blending manner, however, it is fitting to be mindful both here and in all cases, conjecturing—if the stars that have taken the lordships of the places sought happen to be not uniform but different or productive of opposite things—which of them, from the advantages of power that accrue to each, are found to have more votes toward the prevalence of what shall be accomplished; so that either we make the examination consistent with their natures, or, the votes being of equal weight, when those that prevail are together, we reckon out skilfully what is gathered from the blending of the different natures; but when they stand apart, we distribute to each, part by part, in their own times, the events proper to them—to the eastern ones rather earlier, to the western later. For from the beginning it is necessary that a star which is to accomplish anything concerning the sought place be made kindred to it; and this not having happened, it is impossible at all for one who has not shared in the beginning to dispose anything great; but for the time of the outcome in the event, the cause is no longer that of the first lordship, but the distance of the one that has somehow taken the lordship, with respect to the sun and the corners of the cosmos.
Concerning the quality of action

The planet that holds the rulership of action is taken in two ways, from the Sun and from the sign at midheaven. For one must observe both the planet that has made its morning appearance nearest the Sun and the one upon the midheaven, especially when it holds the application of the Moon. And if it is the same planet that has both of the things mentioned, it alone must be used; likewise, if no planet has the one quality, the planet that alone has the other must be used. But if the planet that has made the nearest appearance is one, and another is allied to the midheaven and the Moon, both must be used, giving the priority to the one that has more votes of rulership by prevailing, in the manner we set out earlier. And if no planet is found either to have made its appearance or to be upon the midheaven, the ruler of the midheaven must be taken, but with reference to pursuits according to the occasion; for such men as a rule become inactive.

The planet, then, that has taken the rulership of action will be distinguished by us in this way; and the quality of the actions comes both from the particular nature of the three planets Mars, Venus, and Mercury, and from that of the signs through which they happen to be passing. For Mercury, when he furnishes the activity, makes — to put it in outline — secretaries, men of business, accountants, teachers, merchants, bankers, diviners, astrologers, sacrificers, and in general those who work from letters and interpretation and giving and receiving. And if Saturn bears witness to him, he makes stewards of other men's property, or interpreters of dreams, or those who frequent temples on the pretext of divinations and inspired frenzies; but if Jupiter does so, lawgivers, orators, sophists, men who keep company with greater persons.

Venus, when she furnishes the activity, makes those whose work lies among the scents of flowers or perfumes, or among wines, or colors, or dyes, or aromatics, or ornaments — such as perfumers, garland-weavers, tavern-keepers, wine-merchants, druggists, weavers, dealers in aromatics, painters, dyers, clothing-sellers. And if Saturn bears witness to her, merchants in articles of luxury and adornment, but also sorcerers and poisoners and procurers and those who make their gain from such practices; but if Jupiter does so, crowned athletes, men accounted worthy of honors, and those advanced by women.

Mars, when configured with the Sun, makes those who work by fire, such as cooks, smelters, men who burn, coppersmiths, miners; but when found apart from the Sun, those who work by iron, such as shipwrights, builders, farmers, quarrymen, stonecutters, stoneworkers, woodcleavers, laborers. And if Saturn bears witness to him, sailors, bilge-drainers, sewer-cleaners, dyers, keepers of beasts, cooks, butchers; but if Jupiter does so, soldiers, attendants, tax-collectors, innkeepers, ferrymen, sacrificers.

Again, when two of the planets that furnish the actions are found together: if Mercury and Venus take the rulership, they direct the actions toward the Muse and instruments and melodies, or poems and rhythms, and especially when they have shared the places between them; for they make musicians of the theater, actors, dealers in slaves, instrument-makers, dancers, makers of strings, painters, dancers, weavers, wax-modelers. And if Saturn in turn bears witness to them, he makes those who deal in the kinds named and in the ornaments of women; but if Jupiter does so, advocates, men set over counting-houses, those occupied in public affairs, teachers of children, leaders of crowds.

But if Mercury and Mars together take the rulership of action, they make sculptors, makers of arms, engravers of sacred figures, modelers of figures, wrestlers, physicians, surgeons, accusers, adulterers, evildoers, forgers. And if Saturn bears witness to them, murderers, clothes-stealers, robbers, brigands, cattle-rustlers, knaves; but if Jupiter does so, lovers of arms or of single combat, men of action, formidable, busy in affairs, who attack others and make their gain by such means.

But if Venus and Mars together take the rulership of action, they make dyers, perfumers, tin-workers, lead-workers, goldsmiths, silversmiths, farmers, dancers in arms, makers of drugs, and physicians who use drugs in their cures. And if Saturn bears witness to them, attendants of sacred animals, embalmers of the dead, dirge-singers, players at tombs, men possessed by frenzy, those who pass their lives where there are mysteries and dirges and shedding of blood; but if Jupiter does so, temple-servants, augurs, sacred bearers, men set over women, interpreters of marriages and unions, who live by such means, in a manner at once given to pleasure and reckless of danger.
