And the particular natures of the signs in which the planets that furnish the activity happen to be also contribute something to the variety of the actions. For the signs of human shape cooperate in a way toward all the scientific occupations and those concerned with human service; the four-footed signs toward those of mining and trade and building and carpentry; the tropic and equinoctial signs toward those of interpretation and exchange and measuring and agriculture and priestly office; the land and the watery signs toward occupations in or by water, and toward those of plants and shipbuilding, and further toward burials or saltings or fishing.

And in particular again, if the Moon holds the place of action, making her course from conjunction together with Mercury: in Taurus and Capricorn and Cancer she makes diviners, sacrificers, dish-diviners; in Sagittarius and Pisces, necromancers and those who move spirits; in Virgo and Scorpio, magicians, astrologers, men who utter oracles and have foreknowledge; in Libra and Aries and Leo, men inspired by the god, interpreters of dreams, exorcists.

The form of the actions themselves, then, must be conjectured by such means according to the mixture of the temperament; but their magnitude from the power of the ruling planets. For when these are oriental or at an angle, they make the actions authoritative; when occidental or declining from the angles, subordinate. And dominated by benefics, the actions are great and glorious and profitable and unfailing and graced with charm; dominated by malefics, they are humble and inglorious and unprofitable and precarious — Saturn in opposition bringing coldness and dimness, Mars rashness and notoriety, and both of them complete overthrows. The general time of the increase or, again, of the humbling is to be observed from the constant disposition of the planets that are causes of the result toward the eastern and western angles.
On the beneficent and the maleficent

These things being so, since of the four humours two are fertile and productive, that of the hot and that of the moist (for through these all things are compounded and increased), and two are destructive and passive, that of the dry and that of the cold (through which all things in turn are dissolved and decay), the ancients received two of the planets, that of Jupiter and that of Venus, and also the moon, as beneficent, because of their good temperament and their having the greater part in the hot and the moist; and the star of Saturn and that of Mars as productive of the opposite nature, the one because of its excessive cold, the other because of its excessive dryness. The sun and the star of Mercury, because of the commonness of their natures, they held to be capable of both, and rather to be turned in whichever direction they are joined with the others.
On the examination of the countries affected

Concerning the first and local part, then, we shall make our determination thus. At the eclipse-bearing conjunctions of sun and moon that occur, and especially the more perceptible ones, we shall examine the eclipse-bearing place of the zodiac and the countries kindred to the triangles upon it; and likewise which of the cities, whether from the horoscope and the position of the lights at their founding, or from the midheaven of those then ruling, have sympathy with the sign of the eclipse. For as many countries or cities as we find with the said kinship, in all of them generally one must suppose that some event will occur, but most of all in those that have a relation to the very sign of the eclipse, and in which the eclipse appeared above the earth.
On brothers and sisters

The place concerning parents, then, would become nearly evident to us from these things. As for that concerning brothers and sisters, if here too one should examine the general only, and not, beyond the possible, inquire accurately and in particular into the number, it would be taken more naturally as concerning those of the same mother only, and from the culminating sign of the maternal place—that is, the one containing by day Venus, by night the moon—since this sign and the one rising after it become the place concerning children of the mother, which ought to be the same as the place of the one born concerning brothers and sisters. If, then, benefics be configured with the place, we shall declare an abundance of brothers and sisters, making our conjecture both toward the multitude of the stars themselves, and whether they happen to be in single-formed signs or in bicorporeal ones. But if the malefics overcome them, or also oppose them in diameter, they are indicative of fewness of brothers and sisters, and most of all if they take the sun together with them; and if the opposition occur also at the angles, and especially of the horoscope, in the case of Saturn they become first-born or first-reared, but in the case of Mars they have few brothers and sisters through the death of the rest. Moreover, of the stars that give brothers and sisters, if they happen to be well disposed cosmically, those given are to be reckoned well-figured and glorious; but if the contrary, lowly and inconspicuous; and if the malefics overcome the givers, or rise after them, also short-lived. Those cosmically masculinized will give males, the feminized females; and again the more eastern will give the elder, the more western the younger. Besides these, if the givers of brothers and sisters happen to be harmoniously configured with the lord of the sign concerning brothers and sisters, they will make the brothers and sisters given affectionate; and if with the Lot of Fortune, also living in common; but if they happen to be in unconnected places, or in the opposite station, hostile, envious, and generally treacherous. It would remain, if one should busy himself with the particulars about each of them, that here too in turn they may be conjectured, the giving star being laid down according to the method of the horoscope, and the rest observed together as at a nativity.
Concerning unions

Next after these comes the account of unions. As for the living-together of man and woman according to law, one must examine it in this way. In the case of men one must look to how the Moon is disposed. For first, when she happens to be in the eastern quadrants, she makes men marry young, or be joined to women younger than their age; in the western quadrants, she makes them marry late, or be joined to older women; but if she is under the beams and configured with Saturn, she makes them altogether unmarried. Then, if she is in a single-form sign and happens to be applying to one of the planets, she makes men marry once; but if she has her application in a bicorporeal or many-formed sign, or to several planets in the same sign, she makes them marry many times. And if the planets that hold the applications, whether by close conjunction or by testimony, happen to be benefics, men take good wives; but if malefics, the opposite. For Saturn, when he holds the application, brings about wives who are laborious and austere; Jupiter, dignified and good managers of a house; Mars, bold and unruly; Venus, cheerful and shapely and graceful; Mercury, intelligent and quick. Further, Venus with Jupiter or Saturn or with Mercury makes them useful in life, loving to their husbands and to their children; but with Mars, passionate and unstable and headstrong.

In the case of women one must look to the Sun. For it too, when it happens to be again in the eastern quadrants, makes the women who have it so disposed either marry young or be joined to younger men; in the western quadrants, marry late or be yoked to older men beyond their own age. And when it is in a single-form sign or applies to one of the morning stars, it makes them marry once; configured in a bicorporeal or many-formed sign, or with several morning stars, it makes them marry many times. So when Saturn is similarly configured with the Sun, they take husbands who are settled and serviceable and industrious; Jupiter, dignified and great-souled; Mars, men of action and unaffectionate and unruly; Venus, neat and shapely; Mercury, useful in life and effective. But Venus with Saturn makes them sluggish and rather feeble in matters of love; with Mars, hot and prone and given to adultery; with Mercury, fluttered about boys. By "eastern quadrants" we now mean, in the case of the Sun, those that lead the rising point of the zodiac and the setting point; in the case of the Moon, those from conjunction and full moon up to the quarters. The western quadrants are those opposite to the ones named.

As a rule, then, the living-together endures whenever the luminaries of both nativities happen to be configured harmoniously — that is, when they are in trine or sextile to one another, and especially when this occurs interchangeably; but much more so when the Moon of the man is in such relation to the Sun of the woman. They are dissolved upon slight occasions, and become wholly estranged, whenever the aforesaid positions of the luminaries fall in disjunct signs, or in opposition, or in quartile. And if the benefic planets regard the harmonious configurations of the luminaries, they preserve the unions sweet and gentle and beneficial; but if the malefics do so, contentious and unpleasant and harmful. Likewise, even in the case of the inharmonious positions, the benefics, by bearing witness to the luminaries, do not wholly cut off the living-together, but bring about returns and reconciliations that preserve gentleness and affection; the malefics, however, bring about the dissolutions with some abuse and insolence. And if Mercury alone is with them, the parties are involved in scandals and accusations; but with Venus, in adulteries or poisonings or the like.

Unions that have come about in any other manner must be distinguished by looking to the planet Venus and the planet Mars and the planet Saturn. For when these are properly joined with the luminaries, the cohabitations are proper and the kinships lawful; for Venus has a kind of kinship with each of the planets named — with Mars by reason of the prime of life that they share in common, since they have their exaltations in signs that are in trine to one another, and with Saturn by reason of the more advanced age, since again they have their houses in signs that are in trine to one another.

Hence Venus with Mars makes simply amorous dispositions; with Mercury also present, scandals as well; in the signs that are common and allied to both, Capricorn and Pisces, unions with sisters or kinswomen. And if in the case of men she accompanies the Moon, she makes them come together with two sisters or kinswomen; but if in the case of women she accompanies Jupiter, with two brothers or kinsmen.

Again, Venus with Saturn makes the cohabitations simply pleasant and steady; with Mercury also present, beneficial as well; but with Mars too added, unstable and harmful and full of jealousy. And if Venus is in like configuration with them, she makes the unions with persons of the same age; but if she is more to the east than they, with younger men or women; if more to the west, with older women or men. And if Venus and Saturn are in the signs that are common, that is, Capricorn and Libra, they make the unions take place among kinsfolk. And when the aforesaid configuration is at the Ascendant or at midheaven, the Moon, by accompanying it, makes the males come together with mothers or mothers' sisters or stepmothers, and the females with sons or brothers' sons or daughters' husbands; while the Sun, when the planets are especially in the west, makes the males come together with daughters or daughters' sisters or sons' wives, and the females with fathers or fathers' brothers or stepfathers. But if the aforesaid configurations do not fall in the signs of kinship, but are in feminine places, they make men in this way too prone to passion and ready in every way both to act upon and to be acted upon; and in certain formations they make them licentious, as in the forward and the hinder parts of Aries and of the Hyades and of the Water-Pitcher, and the hinder parts of Leo, and the face of Capricorn. And when the planets are set at the first two angles, the eastern and the southern, they bring such passions wholly into the open and lead men to display them in public places; but at the last two, the western and the northern, they make eunuchs, or men of the court, or barren or imperforate women; and with Mars present, castrated men or tribades.

And in general, what sort of disposition men will have toward matters of love we shall, in the case of men, examine from Mars. For when Mars is separated from Venus and from Saturn but is attested by Jupiter, he makes them pure and dignified in matters of love and aiming only at the natural use; but when found with Saturn alone, he makes them cautious and hesitant and cold. When Venus and Jupiter are configured with him, he makes them easily moved and full of desire, yet self-controlled and restrained and on guard against what is shameful; but with Venus alone, or with Jupiter also accompanying her while Saturn is absent, lustful and slack and providing pleasures for themselves from every quarter. And if of the two planets one is evening and the other morning, men are properly disposed toward both males and females, yet not excessively toward persons of either kind; but if both are evening stars, they are inclined to females only — and when the signs are feminine, they are themselves passive as well; but if both are morning stars, they are diseased in their inclination toward boys only — and when the signs are masculine, also toward males of every age. And if Venus is more to the west, men consort with humble or servile or foreign women; but if Mars is, with women of higher rank or married women or mistresses.

In the case of women, Venus must be examined. For when configured with Jupiter or also with Mercury, she makes them chaste and pure in matters of love; and when Saturn is absent and she is allied with Mercury, she makes them stirred and full of appetite, yet for the most part cautious and hesitant and on guard against what is shameful. But Venus, when joined with Mars alone or configured with him, makes them lustful and prone and rather slack; and if Jupiter too is added to them, then, if Mars is under the beams of the Sun, they consort with slaves or men of lower rank or foreigners; but if Venus is, with men of higher rank or masters, taking the manner of courtesans or adulteresses. And if the planets are made feminine by their places or configurations, the women are inclined only to be acted upon; but if made masculine, also to act upon other women. Saturn, however, when allied with the aforesaid configurations, if he too is made feminine, becomes the sole cause of lewdness; but if he is oriental and made masculine, he sets up women open to reproach, or makes them lovers of such — Jupiter again always contributing to the more decorous form of the passions, but Mercury to the more notorious and more easily disgraced.
On masculine and feminine stars

Again, since the primary kinds of the natures are two, the masculine and the feminine, and of the powers set forth that of the moist substance is most of all feminine (for this part, in general, is more present in all females, the others rather in males), they have reasonably handed down to us the moon and the star of Venus as feminine, because they have the greater share in the moist; and the sun and the stars of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars as masculine; and the star of Mercury as common to both kinds, inasmuch as it is productive equally of the dry and the moist substance. They say, too, that the stars are made masculine and feminine according to their configurations to the sun: being eastern and leading, they are made masculine; being western and following, feminine. And further according to their relation to the horizon: in the configurations from the rising to the mid-heaven, or from the setting to the lower mid-heaven beneath the earth, they are made masculine, as being toward the east; but in the remaining two quadrants, as toward the west, they are made feminine.
On the time of the events accomplished

The second, the temporal chapter, by which it is fitting to determine the times of the significations and the amount of their duration, we shall examine in the following way. Since the eclipses that occur at the same time are not accomplished in all dwellings at the same seasonal hours, and since the solar eclipses, even of the same kind, do not everywhere take an equal magnitude of obscuration nor an equal time of duration, first, according to the eclipse hour in each of the dwellings that have a relation, and the elevation of the pole, we shall dispose the angles as at a nativity; then we shall determine for how many equinoctial hours in each the shadowing of the eclipse extends. For when these have been examined, however many equinoctial hours we find, in a solar eclipse we shall suppose that the event remains for that number of years, and in a lunar for that number of months; the inceptions, however, and the more comprehensive intensifications being observed from the relation of the eclipse-bearing place to the angles. For if the place fall toward the eastern horizon, it signifies the inception of the event within the first four-month period from the time of the eclipse, and the comprehensive intensifications about the first third of the whole time of duration; if toward the midheaven, in the second four-month period and the middle third; if toward the western horizon, in the third four-month period and the last third. The particular slackenings and intensifications are observed from the intervening conjunctions, when they fall upon the places that produce the cause or upon the places configured with them, and from the other passages, when the stars that produce the prediction make their risings or settings or stations or acronychal phases, being configured with the signs that hold the cause; since, when they rise or make their stations, they produce intensifications of the events, but when they set, or are under the sun's rays, or make acronychal precedings, they produce a slackening of what is accomplished.
On males and females

The account concerning brothers and sisters having now been set before our eyes in the fitting and natural manner, it would be next to begin with the things at the very birth, and first to run over the reckoning concerning males and females. This is observed not in a single way nor from any one thing, but from both lights and the horoscope and the stars having a relation to them—especially according to the disposition at the sowing, but more comprehensively also according to that at the bringing-forth. The whole must be observed: whether the aforesaid three places and the stars that rule them are either all, or the most of them, masculinized toward the production of a male, or feminized toward the production of a female; and thus one must declare. One must, however, distinguish the masculinized and the feminized in the manner we laid down in the tabular setting-forth at the beginning of the treatise: from the nature of the signs in which they are, from that of the stars themselves, and further from their relation to the cosmos—since being eastern they are masculinized, but western feminized; and besides these, from their relation to the sun—for again, being eastern they are masculinized, but feminized western. Through all of which it is fitting to conjecture the prevalence of the sex for the most part.
Concerning children

Since to the topic of marriage there follows also that of children, one must observe the planets that are present in or configured with the place at the summit or the one that rises after it — that is, the place of the Good Spirit; or, if there are none, those in the places opposite to them. And one must take the Moon and Jupiter and Venus as bestowers of children, but the Sun and Mars and Saturn as productive of childlessness or fewness of children; while Mercury is common to either party, according to whichever of them he happens to be configured with, a giver when he is oriental but a remover when occidental.

The givers, then, when simply so placed and being alone, give single children; but in bicorporeal and feminine signs, and likewise in the prolific ones such as Pisces and Scorpio and Cancer, they give two or even more. And when made masculine, in masculine signs and in configurations with the Sun, they give males; when made feminine, females; but when dominated by the malefics, or when found in barren places such as Leo or Virgo, they give children indeed, yet not to a happy issue, nor to endurance. The Sun and the malefics, on the other hand, when they hold the aforesaid places, if they are in masculine or barren signs and are not dominated by the benefics, are significant of complete childlessness; but when found in feminine or prolific signs, or attested by the benefics, they give children indeed, yet such as are weak and short-lived. And when both sects have a relation to the child-producing signs, there will be losses of the children given, either of all or of a few, according to the superiorities of those that bear witness in each sect — whichever we find more numerous or more powerful by being more oriental or nearer the angles or dominant or rising afterward. If, then, the planets that have rule over the aforesaid signs are oriental, being givers of children, and are in their own places, they make the children given glorious and conspicuous; but if occidental and in the places of the other sect, humble and obscure. And if they are found in harmony with the Ascendant and the Lot of Fortune, the children are dear to their parents and graceful and inherit their estates; but if disjunct or opposed, contentious and made enemies and harmful and not receiving the estates of their parents. Likewise, if the givers of children are configured harmoniously with one another, the children given remain loving toward their brothers and respectful of one another; but if disjunct or in opposition, they are disposed to enmity and to plotting. And the particular details one might in turn conjecture by using, for each child, the Ascendant of the planet that has made the bestowal and, from its remaining disposition as in a nativity, making the examination of the more general matters.
On diurnal and nocturnal stars

Likewise, since of the things that make up time the two most conspicuous intervals are these—that of the day, which is the more masculine through the heat and activity in it, and that of the night, which is the more feminine through the moistness and restfulness proper to it—they have accordingly handed down as nocturnal the moon and the star of Venus, and as diurnal the sun and the star of Jupiter, and as common to both the star of Mercury, diurnal in the eastern figure and nocturnal in the western. They have also assigned to each of the sects the two of destructive substance, yet no longer according to the same natural causes, but according to the opposite ones. For to things of good temperament the like, being made akin, makes their benefit greater, while to the destructive ones the unlike, being mixed in, loosens much of their harm. Hence they have assigned the star of Saturn, being cold, to the heat of the day, and the star of Mars, being dry, to the moisture of the night; for thus each, gaining due proportion through the mixture, becomes proper to the sect that has furnished the good temperament.
On the kind of things affected

The third chapter being the generic, by which one must determine upon what kinds of things the event will fall, this too is taken through the characteristic and form of the signs upon which the places of the eclipses happen to be, and the stars that take the rulership—both the wandering and the fixed—and the sign of the eclipse and that at the angle before the eclipse. The rulership of these is taken, in the case of the wandering stars, thus: that one which has the most relations to both the places set out—both that of the eclipse and that of the angle following it—according to the nearest and visible applications or separations and the relations of the configurations, and further according to lordship of the houses, triangles, exaltations, and terms, will alone take the rulership. But if the same star is not found lord both of the eclipse and of the angle, two stars are to be taken up together—those that have the more kinships to each of the places, as set out—the lord of the eclipse being preferred. And if more are found of equal claim with respect to each, we shall prefer for the rulership the one that is more at an angle, or more effective, or more of the sect. As for the fixed stars, we shall take up together the one among the bright stars that has been first effective at the very eclipse hour at the foregoing angle-position, according to the visible configurations defined by us in the first treatise among the nine modes, and the one which, in the configuration appearing at the eclipse hour, either rose together with, or culminated together with, the angle that follows the place of the eclipse.

The stars taken up for the cause of the event having thus been observed, let us examine together the forms of the signs in which the eclipse and the stars that take the lordship happened to be, since from their characteristic the quality also of the kinds of things affected is generally taken. For the human-formed signs, both those about the circle through the middle of the signs and those among the fixed stars, make the event fall upon the human race. Of the other land animals, the four-footed signs concern the like among the irrational animals, and the creeping signs concern serpents and the like. And again, the beast-like signs concern the savage animals harmful to the human race, and the gentle signs concern the useful and tame animals that assist toward prosperity, analogously to the several forms—such as horses or oxen or sheep and the like. Further, of the land signs, those more toward the Bears concern sudden movements of the earth, and those toward the south the unexpected outpourings from the air. Again, when the ruling places are in the forms of the winged creatures—such as the Virgin, the Archer, the Bird, the Eagle, and the like—they make the event fall upon birds, and especially those used for human food; and when in the swimming creatures, upon water creatures and fishes. And of these, when in the sea creatures—such as the Crab, the Goat-horned, the Dolphin—upon things of the sea, and also upon the conveyance of fleets; and when in the river creatures—such as the Water-pourer and the Fishes—upon things of rivers and springs; and according to the Argo, upon both kinds. Likewise, when in the tropical or equinoctial signs, they generally accomplish their significations upon the conditions of the air and upon the seasons proper to each of them, and particularly upon the spring and the things that grow from the earth. For when in the spring equinox, they concern the buds of the tree fruits, such as the vine and the fig and the things that ripen with them; when in the summer solstice, the gathering and storing of the fruits already borne, and in Egypt particularly the rising of the Nile; when in the autumn equinox, the sowing and the fodder and such things; when in the winter solstice, the vegetables and the kinds of birds or fishes that abound at that season. Further, the equinoctial signs signify upon things sacred and upon the worships of the gods; the tropical, upon the changes of the air and of the accustomed civil usages; the fixed, upon foundations and buildings; the bicorporeal, upon both men and kings. Likewise, those that have their position more toward the risings at the time of the eclipse signify what shall be concerning the fruits, the young in age, and foundations; those toward the midheaven above the earth, concerning things sacred and kings and the middle age; those toward the settings, concerning the changes of laws, the old in age, and the departed.

And concerning what portion of the underlying kind the disposition will reach, both the magnitude of the obscuration of the eclipses suggests it, and the relations of the stars that produce the cause to the eclipse-bearing place. For when configured western with respect to solar eclipses, or eastern with respect to lunar, they generally dispose toward the lesser; when in opposition, toward the half; but when configured eastern with respect to solar eclipses, or western with respect to lunar, toward the greater.
On twin births

And concerning those born two or even more at a time, one must observe likewise the same two places—that is, the two lights and the horoscope. This event is wont to follow upon the blendings whenever the two or also the three places contain bicorporeal signs, and especially when the stars that rule them suffer the same thing, or some are in bicorporeal signs, and some lie two together or even more. And when both the ruling places are in bicorporeal signs and several stars are at the same time configured together, then more than two also befall to be conceived—the multitude being conjectured from the star making the characteristic of number, and the sex from the stars configured together with the sun and the moon and the horoscope toward the production of a male or a female, according to the modes stated in what precedes. And when such a disposition does not include the angle of the horoscope together with the lights, but that of the midheaven, such mothers generally conceive twins or also more. Particularly, three males they bring fully to birth when Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are configured in bicorporeal signs together with the aforesaid places—as under the nativity of the Anaktores; and three females under that of the Graces, Venus, the moon, with Mercury feminized; two males and one female under that of the Dioscuri, Saturn, Jupiter, Venus; two females and one male under that of Demeter and Kore, Venus, the moon, Mars. In which cases it is wont generally to befall that the births are not brought to completion, and that they are brought forth with certain bodily marks, and further that certain extraordinary and unexpected things befall the places, through the appearance, as it were, of such events.
Concerning friends and enemies

Of friendly dispositions and their opposites — of which we call the greater and lasting ones sympathies and enmities, and the lesser and temporary ones associations and disputes — our examination will be in this manner. For in those that are observed through great events, one must attend to the most authoritative places of both nativities — that is, the solar and the lunar and that of the Ascendant and that of the Lot of Fortune. For when these fall in the same twelfth-parts, or have exchanged places, whether all of them or the greater number — and especially when the rising points are about seventeen degrees apart from one another — they make sympathies that are unfailing and indissoluble and free from injury; but when set in disjunct or opposed positions, they make the greatest and most lasting enmities and oppositions. And when they fall in neither relation, but only in those that are configured: if they are in trine or sextile, they make the sympathies weaker; if in quartile, the antipathies weaker — so that at certain times there arise, in the case of friendships, silences and pettinesses whenever the malefics pass over the configuration, and in the case of enmities, truces and reconciliations according to the entries of the benefics into the configurations. And since there are three kinds of friendship and enmity — for men are thus disposed toward one another either through choice, or through use, or through pleasure and pain — when all or most of the aforesaid places are allied to one another, the friendship is composed of all the kinds, just as the enmity is when they are unallied. But when only the places of the luminaries are so, the friendship is through choice, which is the best and most secure friendship, and the enmity the worst and most faithless; likewise, when the places of the Lots of Fortune are so, it is through use; and when those of the Ascendants are so, through pleasures or pains.

One must also observe, of the configured places, the dominations and the regards of the planets. For in whichever of the nativities the domination of the configuration is, or in whichever the same or the nearest sign is at the rising-after, to that one must assign the more authoritative and more controlling part of the friendship or the enmity; and in whichever of them the regard of the planets is better with respect to beneficence and power, to those must be assigned both the more profitable part of the friendship and the more corrective part of the enmity.

In the case of the temporary associations and oppositions that are formed at certain times, one must attend to the motions of the planets in each nativity — that is, at what times the prorogations of the planets of the one nativity come upon the places of the planets of the other. For in accordance with these there arise partial friendships and enmities, lasting the shortest time, namely until the dissolution of the prorogation itself, but the longest time until the arrival of some other of the planets that are borne on. So Saturn and Jupiter, when they come upon one another's places, make friendships through partnerships or agriculture or inheritances; Saturn and Mars, fights and plots by deliberate choice; Saturn and Venus, unions through persons of the kindred, which, however, soon cool; Saturn and Mercury, cohabitations and partnerships through giving and receiving and trade or mysteries; Jupiter and Mars, companionships through dignitary or administrative affairs; Jupiter and Venus, friendships through feminine persons, or through temple-worship or oracles or the like; Jupiter and Mercury, associations through eloquence and the sciences and the philosophical bent; Mars and Venus, unions through love-affairs and adulteries or illicit connections, but precarious and not long flourishing; Mars and Mercury, enmities and scandals and lawsuits through business or the giving of drugs; Venus and Mercury, cohabitations through some art or the Muse, or partnership arising from letters or from feminine persons.

Now the intensification and relaxation of the associations or oppositions, toward more or less, must be distinguished from the disposition of the places that take them over toward the first and most authoritative four places. For when they fall upon the angles or the Lots or the luminaries, they make the signs more conspicuous; but when estranged from these, inconspicuous. And the intensification toward what is more harmful or more profitable to the companions must be distinguished from the particular nature, toward good or evil, of the planets that regard the aforesaid places.

In particular, the place or account concerning slaves, and of the sympathy or antipathy of masters toward them, is taken from the sign of bad fortune, and from the natural suitability of the planets that regard the place, both at the nativity itself and according to the entries or transits in opposition — and especially when the rulers of the twelfth-part either agree with the authoritative places of the nativity or make configurations opposed to them.
On the power of the configurations to the sun

Now further, in accordance with their configurations to the sun, the moon and the three of the wandering stars receive a more or a less in their own proper powers. For the moon, in her increase from rising to the first half-moon, is more productive of moisture; from the first half-moon to the full, of heat; from the full to the second half-moon, of dryness; and from the second half-moon to her hiding, of cold. The wandering stars, when eastern only, from their rising to their first station are more moistening; from the first station to their evening rising, more heating; from the evening rising to the second station, more drying; from the second station to their setting, more cooling. And it is plain that, blended with one another too, they work out a great multitude of differences of qualities in the heavens about us, the proper power of each prevailing for the most part, but turned as to quantity by the power of those configured with it.
On the quality of the event itself

The fourth chapter is that concerning the quality of the event itself—that is, whether it is productive of goods or of their opposites, and of what kind in each direction, according to the characteristic of its species. This is grasped from the productive nature of the stars that ruled the dominant places, and from the blending both with one another and with the places in which they happen to be. For the sun and the moon are the marshals and, as it were, the leaders of the rest, being themselves the cause of the whole working, and of the rulership of the stars, and further of the strength or feebleness of those that rule. And the conjoint view of those that have taken the lordship shows the quality of the events.

We shall begin with the productive characteristic of each of the wandering stars, premising this in common, for the sake of summary recollection: that whenever we speak generally of the blending of one of the five stars, the productive power of the like nature is also to be understood, whether the star itself be in its own condition, or one of the fixed stars or of the places of the zodiac be observed according to its own blending; just as if the appellations were of the natures and qualities themselves and not of the stars. And in the blendings, again, one must consider not only the mixture of the wandering stars with one another, but also that with the fixed stars or places of the zodiac that share the same nature, according to their demonstrated kinships with the planets.

The star of Saturn, then, taking the rulership alone, is in general the cause of destruction through cold; and, in particular, when the event concerns men, it produces long sicknesses, consumptions, wastings, troubles of the humors, fluxes, quartan attacks, exiles, poverty, imprisonments, mournings, fears, and deaths—especially of those advanced in age. Of the irrational animals, it concerns the useful ones generally, producing scarcity and bodily and sickness-bringing destructions of those that exist, by which the men who use them are also affected together and perish. As to the condition of the air, it produces fearful, freezing colds, mists, and pestilence, foul air, cloudiness, and gloom; further, a multitude of snows, not good but destructive, from which also the things that harm human nature among the creeping creatures are bred. As to rivers or seas, in general winters and shipwrecks of fleets and difficult sailing and scarcity and destruction of fishes; in particular, in seas, ebbs and back-flows, and in rivers excessive flooding and the worsening of the river waters. As to the fruits of the earth, want and scarcity and loss, especially of those that serve necessary needs, whether through caterpillar or locust, or floods of waters, or downpours of rain, or hail, or the like, so as even to reach famine and such destruction of men.

The star of Jupiter, obtaining the lordship alone, is in general productive of increase; and, in particular, when the event concerns men, it accomplishes glories, prosperity, abundance, peaceful conditions, and increases of the necessities of life, good states both of body and of soul; further, benefactions and gifts from those in power, and increases, greatness, and magnanimity of those rulers themselves. In general it is the cause of happiness. As to the irrational animals, it makes those for human use plentiful and numerous, and brings destruction and loss to those of the contrary sort. It makes the condition of the air well-tempered, healthful, breezy, moist, and nourishing to the things on earth, and produces good sailing of fleets, moderate floodings of rivers, abundance of fruits, and such things as are like these.

The star of Mars, taking the rulership alone, is in general the cause of destruction through dryness; and, in particular, when the event concerns men, it produces wars, civil discords, captivities, enslavements, uprisings, the wrath of rulers, and the sudden deaths that come through such things; further, fevers and tertian attacks, raisings of blood, and swift violent deaths, especially of those in their prime; likewise acts of violence, insolences, and lawless deeds, conflagrations, murders, robberies, and plunderings. As to the condition of the air, burning heats, hot pestilential and consuming winds, the discharges of thunderbolts and whirlwinds, and droughts. As to the sea, sudden shipwrecks of fleets through disordered winds or thunderbolts or the like; and as to rivers, failures of water, dryings-up of springs, and the spoiling of the drinking waters. As to the things on earth serviceable for human use, of both the irrational animals and the things that grow from the earth, scarcity and destruction of fruits, arising either from the burnings of heat, or from blight, or from the shaking of the winds, or from the burning-up that occurs in the storehouses.

The star of Venus, becoming lord alone of what happens, in general accomplishes things like those of Jupiter, with a certain charm; and, in particular, as to men, glories, honors, joys, prosperity, good marriages, abundance of children, and contentment in every union, increases of possessions, clean and well-ordered ways of life, and reverence toward sacred things; further, good states of body, and kinships with those in power, and the favor of rulers. As to the winds of the air, well-temperings, and moist and most nourishing conditions, good air and clear skies, and abundant rains of fertile waters, good sailing of fleets, successes and gains, and full floodings of rivers; further, it produces especially the abundance, fruitfulness, and benefit of the useful animals and of the fruits of the earth.

The star of Mercury, taking the rulership, in general, according as it is blended with each of the others, is made kindred to their natures; in particular, it is more than all stirring, and in human events it is sharp and most effective and inventive toward the matter at hand; productive of robberies, thefts, piratical raids and assaults, and further of difficult sailing, in its configurations with the maleficent stars; the cause of dry sicknesses, quotidian attacks, coughings, raisings, and consumptions; and effective also of the things that happen concerning the sacred discourse and the worships of the gods, and the royal revenues, and the change of customs or laws from time to time, fittingly to the blending of the stars with them on each occasion. As to the surrounding heavens, being rather dry and easily moved through its nearness to the sun and the swiftness of its return, it is most of all stirring of disordered, sharp, and easily changing winds, and is reasonably productive of thunders, whirlwinds, chasms, earthquakes, and lightnings; and through these it is sometimes productive of the destruction of the useful among animals and plants, and depriving of waters and rivers at its settings, but filling them at its risings.

Particularly, then, each star, when it meets with its own nature, accomplishes such things; but when blended one with another, according to the configurations and the changes of the signs and the phases with respect to the sun, it takes its blending in its workings analogously also, and produces the characteristic concerning the event, varied as it is, mixed from the natures that have shared in it. But since it is boundless and impossible to set down in memoranda the particular event of each blending, and to go through, in such manifold conception, all the configurations of whatsoever kind, this sort of thing would reasonably be left to the application and ingenuity of the mathematician with respect to particular distinctions.

One must observe also how the stars that have taken the lordship of the prediction are disposed in kinship toward the very countries or cities upon which the event is signified. For when they are beneficent stars and kindred to the things affected, and not overcome by stars of the opposite sect, they accomplish still more of what is, by their own nature, useful; just as, when not kindred, or when overcome by the opposing stars, they are of less benefit. And when they are of the harmful blending and have taken the lordship of the prediction, if they happen to be kindred to the things affected, or are overcome by stars of the opposite sect, they harm less; but if they neither have the rulership of the countries nor are overcome by those fittingly disposed toward them, they bring down the destructiveness of their blending more violently. Generally, however, those men fall together into the universal sufferings who, in their own nativities, happen to have the most necessary places—I mean those bearing the lights, or those of the angles—the same as the stars that produced the cause of the universal events, that is, the same as the eclipse-bearing places or their diameters. And of these, the most perilous and hard to guard against are the degree-by-degree holdings or diametrical oppositions of the eclipse-bearing places with respect to either of the lights.
On monstrous births

Not foreign to the present examination is also the account concerning monstrous births. For first, in such cases, the lights are for the most part found declining or unconnected with the horoscope, and the angles occupied by the malefics. When, then, such a disposition falls under the eye—since it occurs often also about lowly and ill-starred nativities, even though they be not monstrous—it is fitting at once to examine the preceding conjunction, whether new-moon or full-moon, and the star that ruled it and the lights of the bringing-forth. For if the places of the lights of the bringing-forth, and that of the moon and that of the horoscope, all or the most of them, happen to be unconnected with the place of the preceding conjunction, the one born must be supposed enigmatic. If, then, these being so, the lights are also found in four-footed or beast-like signs, and the two malefics are at the angles, the one born will not even be of human kind: but with no benefic bearing witness to the lights, and the malefics doing so, it will be wholly savage and of those that have a wild and harmful nature; but with Jupiter or Venus bearing witness, of those that are deified, such as dogs or cats or the like; and with Mercury, of those serviceable for human use, such as birds or swine or oxen or goats and the like. But if the lights be taken in human-shaped signs, the rest being likewise, the things born will be by men or among men, but monstrous and enigmatic in their special quality—here too observed together from the form of the signs in which the malefics that occupy the lights or the angles happen to be. If, then, here too not one of the benefic stars bears witness to any of the aforesaid places, they become wholly irrational and truly enigmatic; but if Jupiter or Venus bear witness, the special character of the monstrous birth will be honored and well-figured—such as is wont to occur about hermaphrodites, or those called of Harpocrates, and the like. And if Mercury also bear witness, together with these, it makes them given to utterance and provided for through such things; but Mercury alone makes them toothless and deaf, yet otherwise gifted and cunning.
Concerning travel abroad

The topic of travel abroad is determined through the position of the luminaries with respect to the angles — of both, but especially of the Moon. For when she is setting or declining from the angles, she brings about travels and changes of place. And sometimes Mars can do the like, when he is either setting or himself declining from the place at the summit, whenever he has an opposition or quartile relation to the luminaries. And if the Lot of Fortune too falls in the signs that produce the departure abroad, men continue to have their whole livelihood and their occupations and their actions in a foreign land. So when benefics regard the aforesaid places or are borne upon them, men will have glorious and profitable undertakings abroad, and returns that are swift and unhindered; but when malefics do so, undertakings that are laborious and harmful and dangerous and from which it is hard to return — the examination of the mixture being everywhere taken into account, according to the prevalence of the planets configured with these same places, as we determined at the outset.

As a rule, when the luminaries fall in the declines of the eastern quadrants, the departures come to pass toward the eastern and southern regions of the inhabited world; when in those of the western, or in the very point of setting, toward the northern and western. And if the signs that produce the travel abroad are single-form — whether they themselves or the planets that rule them — men will make their departures after a long interval and according to occasions; but if bicorporeal or two-formed, continually and for the greatest length of time.

Jupiter, then, and Venus, when they become rulers of the places and luminaries that produce the travel, make the journeys not only free from danger but also agreeable; for men are escorted on their way either by the magistrates in the countries or by the favors of friends, with the wholesomeness of the climates and the abundance of necessities cooperating with them. And when Mercury too is added to them, often through that very meeting profits and advancements and gifts and honors accrue. But Saturn and Mars, when they take over the luminaries — and especially when they are in opposition to one another — make what is left over useless and involve men in great dangers: when found in watery signs, through difficult voyages and shipwrecks, or again through hard roads and desert places; in solid signs, through fallings from heights and the assaults of winds; in tropic and equinoctial signs, through want of necessities and pestilential conditions; in signs of human shape, through robberies and plots and plunderings; in land signs, through the onsets of beasts or earthquakes; and with Mercury also present, through false accusations and dangerous indictments, and further through the strokes of serpents and of other venomous creatures — while there is observed, besides, the particular nature of the events, whether they be profitable or harmful (that is, the difference touching their cause), and the rule of the causal places of action or possessions or body or dignity according to the original disposition; and the seasons that will most produce the marked occurrences are determined from the quality of the entries of the five planets according to the times. And let these matters be sketched by us to this extent.
On the power of the fixed stars

It being next in order to run over the natures of the fixed stars also according to their own special productive power, we shall set forth the characters observed in them, making our exposition like that of the natures of the wandering stars. And first of those whose forms lie about the very circle through the middle, the zodiac.

Of the Ram, then, the stars in the head have a productive power like that of a mixture of the powers of Mars and Saturn; those in the mouth, like that of Mercury and mildly of Saturn; those in the hind foot, like that of Mars; and those on the tail, like that of Venus.

Of the stars in the Bull, those on the line of section have a temperament like that of Venus and mildly of Saturn; those in the Pleiades, like that of the moon and Jupiter; of those in the head, the bright one of the Hyades, somewhat ruddy, called the Torch-bearer, is like Mars, but the rest like Saturn and mildly Mercury; and those at the tips of the horns, like Mars.

Of the stars in the Twins, those on the feet share a quality like that of Mercury and mildly of Venus; the bright ones about the thighs, like Saturn; of the two bright ones in the heads, the one in the leading Twin is like Mercury, and is called the star of Apollo; the one in the following Twin is like Mars, and is called the star of Hercules.

Of the stars in the Crab, the two on the eyes are productive of the same effect as Mercury and mildly Mars; those in the claws, like Saturn and Mercury. The cloudy cluster in the breast, called the Manger, is like Mars and the moon; and the two on either side of it, called the Asses, like Mars and the sun.

Of those about the Lion, the two on the head produce the like of Saturn and mildly of Mars; the three in the neck, the like of Saturn and mildly of Mercury; the bright one on the heart, called Regulus, is like Mars and Jupiter; those in the loins, and the bright one on the tail, like Saturn and Venus; and those in the thighs, like Venus and mildly Mercury.

Of those in the Virgin, the stars in the head and the one at the tip of the southern wing have a productive power like that of Mercury and mildly of Mars; the rest of the bright ones in the wing, and those about the girdle, like Mercury and mildly Venus; the bright one in the northern wing, called the Forerunner of the Vintage, like Saturn and Mercury; the one called the Spike, like Venus and mildly Mars; and those at the tips of the feet and on the train, like Mercury and mildly Mars.
Of the stars in the Claws of the Scorpion, those at their very tips dispose in like manner to Jupiter and Mercury; those in the middle, to Saturn and mildly to Mars.

Of the stars in the body of the Scorpion, the bright ones in the forehead produce the same as Mars and mildly Saturn; of the three in the body, the middle one, ruddy and brighter, called Antares, is like Mars and mildly Jupiter; those in the segments, like Saturn and mildly Venus; those on the sting, like Mercury and Mars; and the so-called cloudy cluster, like Mars and the moon.

Of those about the Archer, the stars on the point of the arrow have a productive power like that of Mars and the moon; those about the bow and the grip of the hand, like Jupiter and Mars; the cluster in the face, like the sun and Mars; those in the cloak and on the back, like Jupiter and mildly Mercury; those in the feet, like Jupiter and Saturn; and the quadrilateral on the tail, like Venus and mildly Saturn.

Of the stars in the Goat-horned, those on the horns act in like manner to Venus and mildly to Mars; those in the mouth, to Saturn and mildly Venus; those in the feet and the belly, to Mars and Mercury; and those on the tail, to Saturn and Jupiter.

Of those about the Water-pourer, the stars in the shoulders dispose like Saturn and Mercury, together with those in the left hand and the garment; those on the thighs, more like Mercury and less like Saturn; and those in the stream of water, like Saturn and mildly Jupiter.

Of those about the Fishes, the stars in the head of the more southern fish produce the same as Mercury and mildly Saturn; those in the body, like Jupiter and Mercury; those on the tail and the southern cord, like Saturn and mildly Mercury; those in the body and the backbone of the northern fish, like Jupiter and mildly Venus; those on the northern part of the cord, like Saturn and Jupiter; and the bright one on the knot, like Mars and mildly Mercury.

Of those in the more northern figures of the zodiac, the bright stars about the Little Bear have a quality like that of Saturn and mildly of Venus; those about the Great Bear, like Mars; the cluster of Berenice's Hair beneath its tail, like the moon and Venus; the bright stars in the Dragon, like Saturn and Mars and Jupiter; those of Cepheus, like Saturn and Jupiter; those about Boötes, like Mercury and Saturn—but the bright and ruddy one, called Arcturus, is like Jupiter and Mars; those in the Northern Crown, like Venus and Mercury; those in the Kneeler, like Mercury; those in the Lyre, like Venus and Mercury, and likewise those in the Bird; those of Cassiopeia, like Saturn and Venus; those of Perseus, like Jupiter and Saturn, while the cluster on the hilt of the sword is like Mars and Mercury; the bright stars in the Charioteer, like Mars and Mercury; those of the Serpent-holder, like Saturn and mildly Venus, and those about his serpent, like Saturn and Mars; those of the Arrow, like Mars and mildly Venus; those about the Eagle, like Mars and Jupiter; those in the Dolphin, like Saturn and Mars; the bright stars of the Horse, like Mars and Mercury; those in Andromeda, like Venus; and those of the Triangle, like Mercury.

Of those in the more southern figures of the zodiac, the bright star in the mouth of the Southern Fish has an effect like that of Venus and Mercury; those about the Sea-monster, like Saturn; of those about Orion, the stars on the shoulders are like Mars and Mercury, the rest of the bright ones like Jupiter and Saturn; of those in the River, the last and the bright one are like Jupiter, the rest like Saturn; those in the Hare, like Saturn and Mercury; of those about the Dog, the others are like Venus, but the bright one in the mouth is like Jupiter and mildly Mars; the bright star in the Forerunner of the Dog is like Mercury and mildly Mars; the bright stars of the Water-snake, like Saturn and Venus; those in the Bowl, like Venus and mildly Mercury; those about the Raven, like Mars and Saturn; the bright stars of the Ship, like Saturn and Jupiter; of those about the Centaur, the stars in the human body are like Venus and Mercury, the bright ones in the horse like Venus and Jupiter; the bright stars about the Beast, like Saturn and mildly Mars; those in the Censer, like Venus and mildly Mercury; and the bright stars in the Southern Crown, like Saturn and Mercury.
Such, then, was the observation that the men of old made of the powers of the stars in themselves.
On the colors of eclipses and comets and such things

For the universal circumstances one must observe also the colors at the eclipses, whether of the lights themselves or of the formations that occur about them, such as rods or halos or the like. For when they appear black or somewhat livid, they are significant of the things said of the nature of Saturn; white, of those of Jupiter; somewhat tawny, of those of Mars; yellow, of those of Venus; varicolored, of those of Mercury. And if the characteristic of color that occurs appears over the whole bodies of the lights, or over the whole regions about them, the event will be over the most parts of the countries; but if over any single part, over that part alone, toward which the inclination of the characteristic is directed.

One must observe further also the appearances of comets that are formed, whether at the eclipse seasons or at any time whatever, with a view to the universal circumstances—such as those called beams or trumpets or jars and the like—as being by nature productive of the characteristics of Mars and Mercury, and of wars and burning or disturbed conditions, and of the things that accompany these. And they declare, through the parts of the zodiac in which their formations appear, and through the inclinations of their tails according to their figures, the places upon which the events fall; through the formations, as it were, of the formation itself, the species of the event and the kind of thing upon which the suffering will fall; through the time of their continuance, the duration of the events; and through their relation to the sun, the inception also—since when they appear eastern for a long time they signify more quickly, but western more slowly.
On those not reared

There remaining, among the things at the very birth, the account concerning those not reared, it is fitting to determine that in one way this manner is held by the account concerning the length of life, since the kind sought is not foreign to either; but in another way it is separated, in that it differs somewhat in the very power of the examination. For the account concerning the length of life is observed in the case of those who altogether have perceptible times—that is, not less than one solar period; for such a time is properly apprehended as a year, but in power that less than this also—months and days and hours. But that concerning those not reared is in the case of those who do not even reach the time set before us, but in the lesser numbers are destroyed through the excess of the harm. Hence the former has the more manifold examination, the latter the more comprehensive. For simply, if either of the lights be at an angle and one of the malefics be conjunct or in opposition—and these by degree and at equal balance—no benefic being configured, and the lord of the lights being held in the places of the malefics, the one born will not be reared, but will have the end of life at once. And if this happen not at equal balance, but the shafts of the malefics come close behind the places of the lights, and there be two malefics, and they harm either one of the lights or also both, whether by post-ascension or by diameter, or in turn the one harming the one and the other the other, or the one harming by diameter and the other by post-ascension—thus also they become timeless, the multitude of the harms doing away with the humanity toward continuance of life that comes from the interval of the post-ascension. The star of Mars especially harms the sun by post-ascension, and Saturn the moon; while by diameter or supremacy, conversely, Saturn harms the sun, and Mars the moon—and most of all if they have control locally, having ruled either the lights or the horoscope. But if there be two oppositions, the lights being at angles and the malefics at equal balance, then the infants are born dead or half-dead. These things being so, if the lights happen to have a separation from one of the benefics, or be otherwise configured with them—these, however, casting their rays into the leading parts of the lights—the one born will live on up to the number between the emission and the nearer rays of the malefics, the months or days or also hours equal to the degrees, with respect to the magnitude of the harm and the power of those producing the cause. But if the rays of the malefics be borne into the leading parts of the lights, and those of the benefics into the following parts, the one born, though exposed, will be taken up and will live. And again, if the benefics configured be overcome by the malefics, to harm and subjection; but if they overcome, to the substitution of other parents. And if one of the benefics make a rising or an application to the moon, and one of the malefics be under a setting, it will be taken up by the parents themselves. In the same manner also in the case of multiple births: if one of the stars configured two or more together be under a setting, something half-dead or a lump of flesh, and imperfect, will be born; but if it be overcome by malefics, what has been brought into being by the cause concerning it will be unreared or timeless.
Concerning the quality of death

There being left, last of all, the examination concerning the quality of deaths, we shall first determine, by the methods worked out in our discussion of the times of life, whether the destruction will be brought about by the prorogation of a ray, or by the descent of the prorogator toward the western point. For if the destruction comes about by prorogation and meeting, one should observe, for the quality of the death, the place of the meeting; but if by the descent toward the setting point, the very place of setting. For whatever kind of planets either are present at the said places, or, if they are not present, are first of the others to be borne upon them, of such a kind one must judge the deaths to be also — the natures of these planets contributing to the variety of the events, together with the planets configured with them and with the particular nature, both by sign and according to the nature of the bounds, of the destructive places themselves.

So Saturn, when he takes the rulership of death, makes the ends come through long diseases, consumptions, fluxes, wastings, agues, affections of the spleen, dropsies, of the bowels, of the womb, and all that are constituted by an excess of the cold. Jupiter makes the deaths to come from quinsy, inflammation of the lungs, apoplexy, spasms, headaches, affections of the heart, and all that follow upon excess or foulness of breath. Mars, from continual and semi-tertian fevers and sudden strokes, affections of the kidneys and of spitting blood, hemorrhages, miscarriages, childbirths, erysipelas, and destructions, and whatever of the diseases brings on death through fiery heat and excess of the hot. Venus makes the deaths through affections of the stomach and the liver and the bowels, and further through ulcers, fistulas, lichens, the giving of drugs, and all the symptoms that are brought about when the moist is in excess or corrupted. Mercury, through manias and ecstasies and melancholies and fallings and epilepsies and diseases of coughing and bringing-up, and all that are constituted when the dry is in excess or corrupted.

Now those depart this life by deaths that are natural to them who pass away in the manner described, whenever the planets that have taken the rulership of death happen to be in their own or their familiar natural condition, dominated by none of those that are able to harm and to make the end more notorious. But men die by deaths violent and conspicuous whenever either both the malefics have rule over the destructive places — whether being present with them, or in quartile, or in opposition — or whichever of them, or both together, take over the Sun or the Moon, or both luminaries; the harm of the death being constituted from their conjunction, its magnitude from the testimony of the luminaries, and its quality again from the joint regard of the remaining planets and from the signs that contain the malefics.

For Saturn, when he stands in quartile or opposition to the Sun against the sect, in solid signs makes men perish by the pressing of crowds or by hangings or by strangulations; and likewise if he is setting while the Moon is borne upon him; in bestial signs, men destroyed by wild beasts; and if Jupiter bears witness while being himself afflicted, men who fight beasts in public places or on appointed days; and when he is at the opposite point of the Ascendant to either of the luminaries, men who perish in prisons. Configured with Mercury, and especially about the serpents in the sphere or the land signs, men who die from venomous bites; and with Venus added to them, by poisonings and the plots of women; in Virgo and Pisces, or in the watery signs, with the Moon configured, men who are drowned and choked beneath the water; and about the Argo, men who fall in with shipwrecks; in tropic or four-footed signs, when he is with the Sun or in opposition, or, instead of the Sun, with Mars, men overtaken by collapses; and if they are at midheaven or at lower midheaven, men hurled down from a height.

Mars, when he stands in quartile or opposition to the Sun against the sect, or to the Moon, in signs of human shape makes men slain in civil seditions or by enemies, or who become self-slayers; and through women, or also slayers of women, when Venus too bears witness to them. And if Mercury is configured with these, men destroyed by pirates or robbers or malefactors; in the signs of severed limbs and the incomplete signs, or at the Gorgon's head of Perseus, men beheaded or with limbs cut off; in Scorpio and Taurus, men who die by burnings or incisions or amputations of physicians, or by spasms; at midheaven or lower midheaven, men set up on crosses, and especially about Cepheus and Andromeda; at the setting point or the opposite of the Ascendant, men burned alive; in the four-footed signs, men who die from collapses and crushings and accidents. And when Jupiter bears witness to him and is afflicted together with him, men perish again by notable condemnations and the wrath of magistrates or kings.

And when the malefics are joined with one another and are thus in opposition over one of the aforesaid causal conditions, they cooperate still more toward the harm of the death — the rule over the quality belonging to the one that happens to be at the very destructive place — or else many, or double, deadly events are brought about, whether in quality or in quantity, when both have a relation to the destructive places. Such men are also left without burial; and they are devoured by beasts or birds whenever the malefics happen to be about the signs of like form, with none of the benefics bearing witness to the place below the earth or to the destructive places. And the deaths take place abroad when the planets that occupy the destructive places fall in the declines, and especially when the Moon too happens to be present at, or in quartile or opposition to, the aforesaid places.
On the power of the seasons and the four angles

The seasons of the year being four—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—spring has the greater part in the moist, because of the diffusion that follows the past cold as the heat begins; summer the greater part in the hot, because of the sun's nearness to the point overhead us; autumn the greater part in the dry, because of the absorption of the moist things that follows the past heat; and winter the greater part in the cold, because the sun is then farthest removed from the point overhead us. For this reason, although the zodiac, being a circle, has by nature no beginning, they suppose the sign that begins from the spring equinox, that of the Ram, to be the beginning of the whole—making the moist excess of spring, as it were, the starting-point of the zodiac as of a living creature; and the remaining seasons in order. For of all living things too the first ages have the greater part of the moist substance, being tender and still delicate, like the spring; the second, up to their prime, have the greater part in the hot, like the summer; the third, already past their prime and at the beginning of decline, have themselves too the greater part now in the dry, like the autumn; and the last, near to dissolution, have the greater part in the cold, like the winter.

Likewise too of the four places and angles of the horizon, from which the winds blowing over the whole regions take their beginnings: that toward the east itself has the greater part in the dry, because, when the sun comes there, the things moistened during the night then first begin to be dried; and the winds blowing from it, which we commonly call apeliotes, are without moisture and drying. The place toward the south is itself the hottest, both because of the fieriness of the sun's mid-heavenings, and because these, owing to the inclination of our inhabited world, incline rather toward the south; and the winds blowing from it, which we commonly call south winds, are hot and rarefying. The place toward the west is itself moist, because, when the sun comes there, the things absorbed during the day then first begin to be moistened again; and the winds borne from it, which we commonly call zephyrs, are fresh and moistening. The place toward the north is itself the coldest, because, owing to the inclination of our inhabited world, the causes of heat in the sun's mid-heavenings stand farthest from it, as though it were the opposite of mid-heaven; and the winds blowing from it, commonly called north winds, are cold and condensing.

The distinction of these things is also useful for being able, in every way and on each occasion, to discriminate the temperaments. For it is easily understood that, in accordance with such states of the seasons, or of the ages, or of the angles, the productive part of the power of the stars is somehow turned: in their own proper states they have a quality less mixed and an activity stronger—as in the hot states those whose nature is to heat, and in the moist states those that moisten—while in the contrary states a quality mixed and weaker, as in the cold states those that heat, and in the dry states those that moisten; and so likewise in the rest, in proportion to the quality blended through the mixture.
On the new moon of the year

The approach for the universal circumstances of countries and cities having been shown, it would remain to set down memoranda also concerning the more particular matters—I mean those accomplished yearly with respect to the seasons—for which examination it would be fitting to determine beforehand also concerning what is called the new moon of the year. That it is fitting for this to be the beginning of the restoration of the sun in each of its revolutions is plain at once both from its power and from its name. But what beginning one would lay down—in a mere circle simply one could not even conceive; but in the circle through the middle of the signs, one would reasonably take as the only beginnings the points marked off by the equator and the tropics, that is, the two equinoctial and the two tropical points. Here, however, one might already be at a loss which of the four to use as the leading one. By the simple and circular nature, none of them is leading, as upon a single beginning; but those who have written of these matters have used, laying down one thing in different ways, each of the four as a beginning, led by certain proper reasonings and natural sympathies. For each of these parts has something distinctive from which a beginning and a new year would reasonably be reckoned: the spring equinox, because then for the first time the day begins to become greater than the night, and because it is of the moist season, which nature, as we said before, is most present at the beginnings of nativities; the summer solstice, because in it the longest day is accomplished, and among the Egyptians it signifies also the rising of the Nile and the rising of the Dog Star; the autumn equinox, because then the gathering of all the fruits has already taken place, and from another beginning the sowing of the things to come is then cast down; the winter solstice, because then for the first time the magnitude of the day begins to take increase from its diminution. It seems to me more fitting and more natural, for the yearly examinations, to use the four beginnings, observing the conjunctions of sun and moon, whether conjunctive or full-moon, that occur nearest before them, and again, of these, especially the eclipse-bearing ones—so that from the beginning about the Ram we may consider what the spring will be, from that about the Crab the summer, from that about the Claws the autumn, and from that about the Goat-horned the winter. For the general qualities and conditions of the seasons the sun produces, by which even those wholly unskilled in the sciences have a foreknowledge of what is to come.

Further, one must take up also the characteristics of the signs for the signification of winds and of the more comprehensive natures. But the changes from time to time in their greater or lesser degree are shown, in general, by the conjunctions that occur about the points already mentioned and the configurations of the planets with them; and, in particular, by the conjunctions and full moons in each sign and the passages of the stars, which one would call the monthly examination.

Since there ought to be set out beforehand for this purpose also the natural characteristics, part by part, by sign, with respect to the yearly conditions, and further those of each star—the kinship of the planets and of the fixed stars of like blending with the airs and the winds, and further that of the whole signs with the winds and the seasons—we have shown each of these in what precedes. It would remain to speak also of the nature of the signs part by part.
On the length of life

Of the events after the birth the account concerning the length of life leads, since, according to the ancient saying, it is ridiculous to fit the particulars of what is accomplished to one who, from the very ground of the years he is to live, will not at all reach the times of their accomplishment. This account is observed not simply nor unconditionally, but taken in a manifold way from the prevalence of the most authoritative places. The manner that especially agrees with us, and is otherwise according to nature, is of this kind. The whole hangs upon the determination of the prorogative places, and upon the prevailing factors of the prorogation themselves, and further upon the destructive places or stars. Each of these is distinguished thus.

One must reckon as prorogative places, first, those in which absolutely must be that which is to take the lordship of the prorogation: the sign about the horoscope, from the five degrees rising before the horizon itself up to the remaining and rising twenty-five degrees; and the parts to the right of these thirty degrees, sextile to the place of the Good Spirit, square to the midheaven above the earth, trine to the place called God, and diametral to the setting—those being preferred among them, for the power of prevalence, first the ones standing at the midheaven above the earth, then those at the rising, then those at the post-ascension of the midheaven, then those at the setting, then those at the place leading the midheaven. For all that is below the earth must reasonably be rejected from so great a lordship, except only those coming to light at the very rising; and of the part above the earth, it is fitting to take up neither the sign unconnected with the rising one, nor the one that rose before, which is also called that of the Evil Spirit, since it harms the influence onto the earth of the stars in it, together with its declining; and it muddies and as it were obliterates the exhalation from the moist parts of the earth, thick and misty, by reason of which the stars too appear unnatural both in their colors and in their magnitudes.

After these, again, one must take up as prorogators the four most authoritative places: sun, moon, horoscope, Lot of Fortune, and those that rule them. The Lot of Fortune is to be reckoned by the number, always both by night and by day, from the sun to the moon, and carrying the equal amount from the horoscope toward the following parts of the signs, so that whatever relation and configuration the sun has toward the horoscope, this the moon also may have toward the Lot of Fortune, and that it may be, as it were, a lunar horoscope. One must prefer, among these, by day first the sun, if it be in the prorogative places; if not, the moon; if not, the one having more relations of rulership toward both the sun and the preceding conjunction and toward the horoscope—that is, when, the modes of rulership being five, it has three toward one or also more of the said places; if not, last, the horoscope. By night, first the moon, then the sun, then the one having more relations of rulership toward both the moon and the preceding full moon and the Lot of Fortune; if not, last, the preceding syzygy being a new moon, the horoscope, but being a full moon, the Lot of Fortune.
